t: Installation and setup
x: queryapigate serve uses Flask's development server. For production use gunicorn with one worker and several threads, behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy - one worker because /metrics is per process (a scraper would reach one worker at random), and, without Redis, so are rate limits. For more capacity run more instances, each with one worker (Scaling out): pip install "queryapigate[server]" QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY=change-me gunicorn --bind 127.0.0.1:5000 --workers 1 --worker-class gthread --threads 8 \ Behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, also set QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY=1 (the number of proxies) so rate limits and redirects use the real client address and scheme. Once every client reaches it over HTTPS, QUERYAPIGATE_HSTS_MAX_AGE (seconds) adds HSTS - only to requests that arrived over HTTPS. Or use the published Docker image (ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate, with a -h2 variant that includes Java) or the Dockerfile - see the README. The image sets gunicorn's worker timeout to 120 seconds; keep it above QUERYAPIGATE_QUERY_TIMEOUT if you run your own gunicorn. For a full production Docker setup - reverse proxy, secrets, backups, monitoring - see DEPLOYMENT.md.

t: Installation and setup
x: A saved query's cache_ttl (see the README) is served from an in-process cache by default - fast, zero setup, but wiped by every restart and never shared if you run more than one instance behind a load balancer. For an OLTP query that gets hit hundreds of times a second, set QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL to point at a Redis instance instead: the cache then survives a restart and is shared across every instance that points at the same Redis, so a cache warmed by one instance serves every instance's traffic instead of each duplicating the same database hits. pip install "queryapigate[redis]" QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379/0 queryapigate serve If Redis is briefly unreachable, a cached response is simply treated as a miss - the query still runs against the real database, it's just not served from cache for that one request. The same QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL also shares rate limits: the server-wide limit per client address and every key's own rate_limit are counted in Redis, so several instances (and queryapigate mcp/events) enforce one budget, not one each. If Redis fails a check, that process counts on its own for a few seconds before trying Redis again - limits stay enforced, per process, rather than lifted or turned into refusals - logs a warning (at most once a minute), counts it in queryapigate_rate_limit_fallbacks_total, and raises the rate_limits_not_shared alert for te

t: Installation and setup
x: Everything QueryAPIGate itself keeps - connections, saved queries and their run history, API keys, roles and the audit log - lives in queryapigate.db, a SQLite file in QUERYAPIGATE_HOME. That is the right default: nothing to install or run, and fast for a single server. Set QUERYAPIGATE_DATABASE_URL to keep all of it in a PostgreSQL database instead when you need: more than one instance - every instance pointed at the same database serves the same connections, saved queries and keys, and a key revoked through one is revoked on all of them at once; the store on a managed database - backed up, replicated and failed over by your existing PostgreSQL setup rather than by copying a file. pip install "queryapigate[postgres]" export QUERYAPIGATE_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://queryapigate:secret@db.internal:5432/queryapigate queryapigate migrate-to-postgres # once: copies this home's queryapigate.db across (optional) queryapigate serve The tables are created automatically on first start. Use a database (or schema) of its own: the account needs to create tables there. To use a schema other than public, add ?options=-csearch_path%3Dmyschema to the URL. migrate-to-postgres copies everything in one transaction and only ever fills an empty database - it refuses, changing nothing, if the target already holds data. queryapigate.db is opened read-only and left as it was; --from PATH copies a differ

x: queryapigate export --out runs a saved query and writes its full result to a file, entirely in-process against QUERYAPIGATE_HOME - no server needs to be running, no HTTP round trip, no API key. It's built for cron, a systemd timer or a Kubernetes CronJob to call, not a scheduler itself - scheduling, retries and failure notification stay exactly where they already work well: queryapigate export top_rented_films --out '/exports/{name}{date}.csv' {name} (the saved query's name) and {date} (YYYY-MM-DD) in --out are filled in; the target directory is created if missing. --format is csv (default), tsv, ndjson or parquet - the same formats ?stream=true supports, since this calls the same streaming code path internally rather than shelling out to curl against itself. --connection overrides the saved query's own default connection; --param name=value (repeatable) supplies a required parameter. The result is written to a temporary file in the same directory and renamed into place only once it's complete, so a failed run never leaves a partial or corrupt file at the final path - and exits non-zero on any failure, so cron's own failure handling (mail, an alerting integration, whatever the operator already has) works unmodified: # crontab: every morning at 6am, mail on failure (cron's own default behaviour) 0 6 * * /usr/local/bin/queryapigate export top_rented_films --out '/exports/{name}_{

t: Configuration
h: Calling the API from a browser
x: Browsers refuse cross-origin JSON calls unless the server allows them. List the sites that may call the API: QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY=change-me QUERYAPIGATE_CORS_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com queryapigate serve Preflight checks are answered automatically, and the pagination headers (X-Has-More etc.) are exposed to the page's JavaScript. CORS only tells the browser which sites may call; it is not authentication, so keep the API key. Avoid * without a key: any website a visitor opens could then reach your databases through their browser (the server logs a warning if you start that way).

t: Configuration
x: QUERYAPIGATE_RATE_LIMIT=60/minute gives each client address a bucket of 60 requests that refills steadily, so short bursts work but the sustained rate is capped. Over the limit, requests get 429 with a Retry-After header, and every response carries X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining. The limit is applied before the API key check, so guessing keys is throttled too; /health and CORS preflights are never counted. With QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL set, limits are counted in Redis - one budget per client address and per key across every instance and process (serve, mcp, events); if Redis fails, each process falls back to counting on its own until it's back, and an alert says so. Without Redis, state is per process: with several workers or instances, the effective limit is multiplied by their number. An API key can also carry its own rate_limit (same grammar), checked in addition to the server-wide limit, never instead of it - a request has to pass both. See Per-key rate limiting.

x: Everything QueryAPIGate owns - connections, saved queries and their versions, run history, API keys, roles and the audit log - lives in its store: queryapigate.db on the /data volume, or a PostgreSQL database if you set one up (section 8). t: Deployment
h: 5. Persistent data, backups and restores › The SQLite store
x: queryapigate backup copies it while the server keeps running. It uses SQLite's own backup API, so the copy is one consistent moment and includes changes still in the write-ahead log (queryapigate.db-wal) - which a plain cp of the file can miss: docker compose exec queryapigate queryapigate backup /data/backup.db --force docker compose cp queryapigate:/data/backup.db "./backups/queryapigate-$(date +%F).db" docker compose exec queryapigate rm /data/backup.db Run that on a schedule (host cron, or a small sidecar with its own) and ship the result off the host. To restore, stop the server, put the backup in place as queryapigate.db - removing the -wal and -shm files, which belong to the store being replaced - and start it again: docker compose stop queryapigate docker compose run --rm -v ./backups:/backups queryapigate sh -c \ 'cp /backups/queryapigate-2026-10-04.db /data/queryapigate.db && rm -f /data/queryapigate.db-wal /data/queryapigate.db-shm' docker compose start queryapigate

t: Deployment
h: 5. Persistent data, backups and restores › The PostgreSQL store
x: Back it up with pg_dump, like any other PostgreSQL data. On a managed database whose snapshots or point-in-time recovery already cover the whole database, that covers QueryAPIGate's store too. To back up just the store, dump its schema - public, or the one ?options=-csearch_path%3D... names in QUERYAPIGATE_DATABASE_URL; queryapigate backup prints this command with the right schema filled in: pg_dump --format=custom --schema=public --no-owner --no-privileges \ pg_dump reads one snapshot, in a single transaction, so it is consistent and safe to run while QueryAPIGate is serving; runs recorded after it starts are simply not in it. Use a pg_dump of the same major version as the server, or newer. To restore, stop every QueryAPIGate process using the store, restore into an empty database (or one where that schema has been dropped), and start them again: pg_restore --no-owner --no-privileges --dbname="$QUERYAPIGATE_DATABASE_URL" "queryapigate-2026-10-04.dump" The schema is recreated under its original name, so the URL's search_path (if any) must name the same schema.

t: Deployment
h: 5. Persistent data, backups and restores › What a backup of the store does not contain
x: QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY, if you set it: connection passwords are stored encrypted with it. A store restored without the same key has every encrypted password unreadable - each connection must be given its password again. Keep the key in your secrets manager, with the .env it lives in. After a key rotation (queryapigate rekey), a backup taken before it still needs the old key: list it after the new one to restore it, then run rekey again. QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY, the admin key, and any environment variable a connection refers to ("password": "${WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD}"). Scoped API keys are in the store - as hashes, so they keep working after a restore, but a lost secret can't be recovered from a backup: issue a new key instead. The databases QueryAPIGate connects to - back those up in their own right. The Redis response cache, if used, is disposable: it refills. A restore from an older release's store is upgraded on first start, as any upgrade is; one from a newer release is refused rather than run on. tests/test_backup_restore.py does all of this on every CI run: it fills a store, backs it up, loses it, restores it, and checks the admin API sees exactly what it saw before.

t: Deployment
x: Read the Changelog entry for the target version, especially anything under a "Breaking" or "Upgrading" heading. Back up first - always, even for a patch version. Bump the pinned tag in docker-compose.yml, then docker compose pull && docker compose up -d. Check docker compose logs queryapigate and curl .../health. The queryapigate.db schema is migrated automatically on the container's first start against it - nothing to run by hand. Every release since 0.7 is tested this way: a store each one built through its own API is started under the current code, which must read back its connections, queries and their versions, run history, keys and roles (tests/test_upgrades.py). A store this version can't safely run on - one with a column missing, or one a newer release has already upgraded - stops startup with a message naming the problem and what to do, before anything is changed; it never starts and then fails on first use. Going back to an older release is not supported in place: restore the backup from step 2.

t: Deployment
h: Upgrading › Rolling upgrades (several instances on one store)
x: Replace instances one at a time - no downtime - because of this rule: within 1.x, a release changes the store only additively (new tables, new nullable columns, new indexes; never a rename, a drop or a changed meaning). One exception, before 1.x: the upgrade to 0.38 (workspaces, ADR 0023) changes the store's primary keys, so stop every 0.37 instance before the first 0.38 one starts - see the changelog. So while some instances run the new release and have upgraded the store, the ones still on the previous release keep working against it. tests/test_rolling_upgrade.py checks exactly that on every CI run: the previous release from PyPI keeps serving, writing and recording runs on a store the current code has just upgraded, and each sees the other's changes. Back up the store. Start one instance on the new version - it upgrades the store on its first start - and check its /health. Replace the others one by one. GET /api/v1/instances shows who is on which version meanwhile. Replace queryapigate events, if you run it, with the instances. From 0.33 it streams the event log (ADR 0020), and an instance still on 0.32 writes its runs to history only - so they aren't events until it's upgraded too. x: MySQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, H2, generic jdbc and duckdb connections are kept open and reused between requests (SQLite is a local file and is opened per request). Tune it with QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_SIZE (idle connections kept per distinct connection setting, default 5, 0 disables pooling) and QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT (seconds, default 300). Clean hand-over. A connection's transaction is ended before it is reused, so a request never sees a stale snapshot, and query limits are applied per request (or per transaction) so they never leak to the next user. Errors. A connection used by a failed or timed-out request is closed rather than reused. Health checks. A connection that sat idle for more than a few seconds is checked before reuse; a dead one is replaced transparently. Changes take effect. Creating, changing or deleting a connection closes all idle pooled connections immediately. If you edit queryapigate.db directly (e.g. via sqlite3), old connections are dropped as they reach the idle timeout. Sizing. The pool bounds idle connections, not concurrent ones. Each server process has its own pool, so the most idle connections your database sees is roughly QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_SIZE x distinct connections x worker processes; keep that below the database's max_connections. Streaming exports hold their connection for the whole download, not just the query. ?stream=true (see Streaming

t: Database connections
x: db: "duckdb" is an embedded analytical database - its own storage, its own .duckdb file, no server process to run - that also reads files directly: Parquet, CSV and JSON, on local disk, object storage or the web. One connection type, two uses: {"name": "analytics", "db": "duckdb", "database": "/data/analytics.duckdb", "active": true} As a general embedded database, it behaves like sqlite: point database at an existing file (QueryAPIGate never creates one, so a mistyped path fails instead of opening an empty database - create it first, e.g. python -c "import duckdb; duckdb.connect('analytics.duckdb')"), then CREATE TABLE/INSERT/SELECT against it as usual. Its SQL dialect is close to PostgreSQL, so it uses the same quote-doubling string-literal rules as postgres/sqlite/h2 (no backslash escaping). Or set database to ":memory:" for a connection that holds no tables of its own - only views over files (below). For files, list what the connection may read in allowed_paths, then read them straight from SQL with DuckDB's own table functions - no import step, column types inferred: {"name": "files", "db": "duckdb", "database": ":memory:", "active": true, "allowed_paths": ["/data/sales/", "/data/reference/countries.csv"]} SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) FROM read_parquet('/data/sales/*.parquet') GROUP BY customer_id SELECT * FROM read_csv('/data/reference/countries.csv') WHERE region = :r

x: These apply to every endpoint that returns rows. | Parameter | Default | Description | | format | json | json, ndjson, csv, tsv, xml, yaml, xlsx or parquet. For the POST endpoints it may also be given in the JSON body. | | page | 1 | 1-based page number. | | page_size | 10 | Rows per page, at most QUERYAPIGATE_MAX_PAGE_SIZE (default 1000). | | timeout | server limit | Seconds the query may run before it is cancelled with a 504. It can lower the server limit (QUERYAPIGATE_QUERY_TIMEOUT, default 30; 0 disables it) but never raise it. For the POST endpoints it may also be given in the JSON body. | Paging happens within the statement's own row window. A query that ends in LIMIT 3 returns at most 3 rows whatever page_size is, and LIMIT 25 with page_size=10 gives pages of 10, 10 and 5, then X-Has-More: false. Every form is understood: LIMIT n [OFFSET m], LIMIT m, n, LIMIT ALL, OFFSET m alone, and [OFFSET m ROWS] FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY. Each number may be a bound :parameter, whose value must then be a non-negative whole number. A LIMIT inside a subquery, a string or a comment is left alone. Responses carry X-Page, X-Page-Size and X-Has-More (true when another page exists). A query that returns no rows answers {"message": "No results returned"}.

x: POST /execute_sql?format=json&page=1&page_size=5 { "sql": "SELECT * FROM film WHERE film_id > :min AND title LIKE :name", "params": {"min": 10, "name": "C%"}, "connection_name": "examples" } :name markers are bound parameters: values are sent to the database separately from the SQL. Unless the server sets QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES=1, only a single SELECT, WITH, SHOW, DESCRIBE, EXPLAIN or VALUES statement is accepted (403 otherwise; 400 for several statements).

t: API reference
x: page_size is capped (QUERYAPIGATE_MAX_PAGE_SIZE, default 1000) - there is normally no way to pull a full result larger than that in one call. ?stream=true lifts that cap: the whole result is streamed straight from the database cursor as it comes in, rather than built up in memory first, so an export far larger than fits in memory can still be downloaded. It works on both POST /execute_sql and GET/POST /q/: curl -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/execute_sql?stream=true&format=csv' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"sql": "SELECT * FROM film", "connection_name": "examples"}' -o film.csv Only format=csv, tsv, ndjson or parquet are streamable (400 for json/xml/yaml/xlsx - those formats all need the whole document structure in memory to write correctly, so paging still applies to them normally). Parquet is written to a temporary file by DuckDB first - its footer comes last - and then sent, so its first byte arrives once the query has finished; memory stays within DuckDB's own, which spills to disk.

x: ?format=parquet (paged or streamed) and queryapigate export --format parquet work on every database type. Column types come from the values: integers BIGINT (DECIMAL(38,0) past 64 bits), floats DOUBLE, decimals DECIMAL(38, scale) - exact, not converted to floats - booleans, DATE, TIMESTAMP (TIMESTAMPTZ with a time zone) and TIME; anything else, or a mix, VARCHAR. A database that returns dates as text (SQLite) gives text columns, as its driver does. Content type application/vnd.apache.parquet. page/page_size are rejected together with stream=true (400) - the whole point is that there is no page. Always read-only, regardless of QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES or the calling key's own write permission - a large export has no business mutating data. A write statement gets the usual 403 from the SQL guard. The response carries Content-Disposition: attachment with a filename, so a browser hitting the URL directly downloads it rather than navigating in-page. For a saved query, the run is still appended to execution_history once the stream finishes, but cache_ttl is ignored - caching would mean building the whole body in memory first, exactly what streaming avoids. x: POST /api/v1/queries creates a saved query with its first version; POST /api/v1/queries/{name}/versions adds the next version (see Management API (v1)): { "name": "film_by_id", "sql": "SELECT * FROM film WHERE film_id = :id", "parameters": {"id": "int"}, "connection_name": "examples", "author": "anantha", "description": "Look up a film", "tags": ["example"], "publish": true } name may contain letters, digits, spaces, ., _ and -. t: API reference
h: Run a saved query › Drafts and publishing
x: Every saved query has at most one published version: the one /q/ runs, and the one the catalog, /openapi.json, MCP tools, Postman and bundle exports describe. A version newer than the published one is a draft, and so is every version of a query with nothing published. A query with nothing published isn't served at all: /q/ answers 404. Drafts are invisible to callers. Only the admin key can run one, and only by asking for it by number (?version=3), to test it before publishing. For any other key, a draft's number answers the same 404 as a version that never existed. Older versions stay runnable with ?version=, as before: each was live once. A new version is a draft unless saved with "publish": true. The Management API also publishes, unpublishes and rolls back to any earlier version. queryapigate collection import and examples load publish what they save. Deleting the published version falls back to the newest version older than it, never to a draft. With none older, the query is left unpublished. GET /api/v1/queries shows each query's published_version (null when nothing is published). Stores created before this (schema 3 and older) are upgraded on first start with every query published at its newest version, so nothing a caller sees changes. POST /execute_sql_from_file and POST /execute_sql_with_parameters_from_file, which ran a saved query named in the body, were deprecated

t: API reference
x: Opt-in, per saved query: set cache_ttl (seconds) when saving it, or turn it on/off or retune it for an existing version in place with PATCH /api/v1/queries//versions/ (admin only, {"cache_ttl": }, 0 or null turns it off) - not a new version, so it never bumps execution_history or the query's version number, the same way moving a query's collection doesn't. A cached response is only ever served for that exact name, version, connection, resolved parameter values, format and page - anything else is a separate entry. It is never used for a query whose SQL is a write (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL), regardless of cache_ttl: caching such a query would silently skip the write on every call after the first. A fresh response carries ETag, Cache-Control: private, max-age= and X-Cache: MISS - private, so the caller's own client may keep it but no shared cache (a CDN, a caching proxy) in front of the server may. A request within the TTL gets the same body with X-Cache: HIT; send back If-None-Match: to get 304 Not Modified with no body instead. A cache hit is not appended to execution_history - nothing ran against the database. The cache is kept in this one process's memory by default, or shared across restarts/instances when QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL is set (see Installation & Setup and the Caching tab in the admin UI) - either way it is shared across every API key that can use the connection, sin

x: A collection is one named group a saved query belongs to - at most one, unlike tags, which are free-form and multi-valued. It exists for three things: browsing (the admin UI groups the API Repository list by collection), access (a key can be granted a whole collection instead of a hand-maintained list of names) and moving queries around as a unit (export and import). Where it lives. On the query's own file, as a top-level "collection" next to the version numbers ({"collection": "reporting", "1": {...}}) - there is no separate registry to fall out of step with the queries. Deleting a query removes its membership; a collection exists exactly while at least one query is in it; moving a query is one atomic file write and not a new version, since the SQL did not change. A hand-edited value that is not a valid name is read as no collection, so a grant can never reach a query through a spelling the API would have refused. Names are 1-63 characters of lowercase letters, digits, ., _ and -, starting with a letter or digit. Anything else - including Reporting - is rejected with 400, never silently case-folded, so two spellings of one collection cannot coexist. Moving a query. PATCH /api/v1/queries/ (admin only) with {"collection": "reporting"}, or {"collection": null} to take it out of any. A new query can also be created into one with collection in POST /api/v1/queries. h: Collections › Granting access to a collection
x: A key (or role) takes a collections list of names: {"name": "acme-corp", "connections": [], "collections": ["reporting"]} It reaches every query currently in those collections, on any connection, and works like queries: additive (it only ever adds reach), read-only, and never ad-hoc SQL. Deliberately: No "*" wildcard. "Every query in any collection" would widen itself with each new collection. No write access through a collection. A write grant stays spelled out per query in queries. Names must exist when granted (400, listing the real ones - a typo would otherwise be a grant that reaches nothing and looks exactly like a working one). Names a key already holds are exempt, so re-saving a key whose collection has since emptied still works. The grant is live, unlike a role, which is copied once. That is the point - nobody maintains a list - and its cost, since filing a query into a collection changes what every key granted it can run. So every move is written to the audit log with the keys that gained or lost access, and GET /api/v1/collections shows who reaches each collection before you move anything. A role's collections are copied onto a key at creation like every other role field. /openapi.json, /catalog and the run path all decide reachability through one function, so a collection grant is honoured (or not) identically by all three - a test compares them across every kind of

t: API reference
x: PATCH /api/v1/collections/ (admin only) with {"name": "new-name"} renames it, carrying every key and role grant with it. It is ordered so that no key loses reach at any moment: grants are widened to hold both names, the queries are re-filed, and only then is the old name dropped. If the process dies part-way, access is never narrower than intended and running the same rename again completes it - which is why an already-existing target requires "merge": true (409 collection_exists otherwise - a half-finished rename looks exactly like one). The response lists the queries, keys and roles changed; the audit log records a rename_collection entry.

An encrypted password is masked the same as a literal one in GET /api/v1/connections/{name} and the audit log () - the stored ciphertext itself is never returned to a client. Losing or rotating QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY fails clearly rather than quietly: a connection whose password can't be decrypted returns a 500 naming the problem, and the server logs a startup warning if encrypted passwords exist on disk but no key is configured to read them - the same "fail closed, say why" precedent expires_at and rate_limit already follow for a key's own malformed data. h: Authentication and permissions › Per-saved-query access (external clients)
x: connections grants a key everything on a connection - every saved query on it, plus ad-hoc SQL if allow_writes and the server allow it. That fits an internal caller, but not an external one who should only ever reach a specific, curated list of saved queries and nothing else on the connection behind them. A key's queries grant covers that case: a list of saved-query names it may run regardless of connections, independent of and additive with whatever connections already allows - never a narrower version of it. A key can have connections: [] (no connection access at all) and still run every query named in queries, but it can never reach ad-hoc SQL through this grant, since queries only ever authorizes the specific named saved query, not the connection behind it - and only on that query's own connection: a request that names a different one with ?connection_name= (or that supplies one for a query with no default) is 403 unless the key also holds a real grant on that connection. h: Authentication and permissions › Per-query write curation
x: A queries entry can be an object instead of a plain name, adding write access to that one query specifically - on top of, never instead of, whatever allow_writes already grants: {"name": "partner", "connections": [], "allow_writes": false, "queries": ["read_orders", {"name": "submit_order", "allow_writes": true}]} Here partner can run read_orders read-only and submit_order (a write) - a single curated write endpoint - with no blanket write access, no connection access, and no ad-hoc SQL of any kind. A plain string entry stays exactly what it always was: read access only. "*" can never carry write access, by design - a key wanting write access to a specific query must enumerate its queries list explicitly rather than hiding a write grant behind a wildcard picked for unrelated read access. Still subject to the usual ceiling: never wider than server-wide QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES, and the query's SQL still has to pass the normal guard (a single statement, actually a write, and - if the key has allowed_write_ops one of the permitted keywords).

x: A key can carry an optional expires_at (YYYY-MM-DD) for time-boxed access - a trial integration, a partner engagement with a known end date - that stops authenticating on its own once the date passes, without anyone having to remember to come back and revoke it: {"name": "trial-partner", "connections": ["reporting-db"], "expires_at": "2026-12-31"} Valid through the end of that date (23:59:59), not from its start. Checked live on every request, the same way active already is - there is no background sweep, so nothing to schedule or fail silently. Omit it (or leave it unset) for a key that never expires; PATCH /api/v1/api-keys/ with {"expires_at": null} clears an existing expiry without rotating the secret, and PATCH without the field at all leaves whatever expiry (or lack of one) the key already had untouched.

x: GET /api/v1/api-keys reports last_used_at for a key once it has authenticated at least one request - useful for noticing a stale key nobody has called in months (a candidate to revoke) or confirming a newly-issued one actually got wired up on the other end. Updated at most once a minute per key regardless of how often it's actually used, so a busy key doesn't turn every request into a disk write - read it as "roughly how recently," not an exact timestamp. A key that has never been used has no last_used_at field at all.

Hand scoped keys to several external clients and they all draw from the same budget - one noisy integration can exhaust it for everyone else. A key's own rate_limit gives it an individual quota instead: {"name": "acme-corp", "connections": [], "queries": ["monthly_revenue"], "rate_limit": "100/minute"} Same N/period grammar as QUERYAPIGATE_RATE_LIMIT (second, minute, hour or day). Checked in addition to the server-wide limit, never instead of it - a key can never use its own quota to exceed the ceiling every caller already sits under, and a per-key limit still applies even when QUERYAPIGATE_RATE_LIMIT is unset entirely, since throttling one specific external caller is a reasonable ask on its own. Omitted (or null) means no limit of this key's own - PATCH /api/v1/api-keys/ with an explicit {"rate_limit": null} clears an existing one, the same pattern expires_at uses.

x: A key can also be pinned to allowed_ips, a list of IP addresses or CIDR ranges (IPv4 or IPv6, mixed freely) it may authenticate from - real defense in depth for a key handed to an external party with known, stable infrastructure, since even a leaked key then only works from an expected address: {"name": "trial-partner", "connections": ["reporting-db"], "allowed_ips": ["203.0.113.5", "198.51.100.0/24"]} Checked against the same client address QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY/ProxyFix already establish as trustworthy for rate limiting, not re-derived here - set QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY correctly behind a reverse proxy, or every caller looks like the proxy's own address. This restricts who may use a key at all, independent of per-key rate limiting above, which restricts how much a caller who is already allowed may do. A request from an address outside the list fails exactly like a wrong key (401), not a distinct error - a caller learns nothing about why a key didn't work. Omitted (or null) means no restriction - the admin key is never restricted by this at all. PATCH /api/v1/api-keys/ with an explicit {"allowed_ips": null} clears an existing restriction, the same pattern expires_at and rate_limit use.

t: API reference
h: Authentication and permissions › Write operation granularity
x: A key with allow_writes on can be narrowed further with allowed_write_ops, a list of the specific SQL statement keywords it may actually perform - INSERT but not DELETE/DROP, for example - rather than every write keyword being equally permitted once writes are on at all: {"name": "ingest-bot", "connections": ["events-db"], "allow_writes": true, "allowed_write_ops": ["insert"]} Only ever narrows write access, never widens it, and never restricts a read-only statement - a key with no allow_writes still can't write regardless of this list. Checked in sqltools.validate_sql() against the statement's own leading keyword (case-insensitive); a rejected statement gets 403 naming the operations the key is permitted. Omitted (or null) means every write keyword is equally permitted, exactly today's behaviour. PATCH /api/v1/api-keys/ with an explicit {"allowed_write_ops": null} clears an existing restriction, the same pattern expires_at/rate_limit/allowed_ips use.

t: API reference
h: Authentication and permissions › Table access restrictions
x: A key can be narrowed to a specific set of tables it may query, allowed_tables - unlike allowed_write_ops, this restricts every statement, read or write, since a table a caller shouldn't see is forbidden regardless of what's being done to it: {"name": "reporting-narrow", "connections": ["reporting-db"], "allowed_tables": ["orders", "customers"]} Needs the sqlglot package to parse SQL (pip install "queryapigate[flow]" - the same optional extra the Access tab's "Query flow" diagram already uses; a query is rejected with 500 if it's missing while a key has allowed_tables set, rather than silently letting the query through unchecked). Checked against every table a statement actually touches - joins, subqueries and CTEs are all resolved correctly (a CTE's own name is never mistaken for a real table), including the target table of a bare DELETE/UPDATE/INSERT. Only supported for mysql, postgres, clickhouse, sqlite and duckdb connections, the dialects QueryAPIGate can actually parse for this - a table-restricted key used against an h2 or jdbc connection is refused on every query, with a 403 naming the unsupported connection type, never silently left unrestricted. On a mongo connection the list is the collections the key may find() in - one outside it is refused with 403 table_not_allowed before the server is asked anything (from 0.34.1; until then it wasn't checked on MongoDB at all).

Anything else (too long, spaces, quotes, non-ASCII) is ignored rather than rejected, and the response header shows the ID actually used. It is a correlation aid only - nothing authorises by it, and two requests may share one if the caller sends the same value twice. Browsers can send and read it cross-origin (X-Request-Id is in the CORS allowed and exposed headers). h: Observability › Seeing it: a built-in view, or a real dashboard
x: The admin UI's Metrics tab reads /metrics itself and renders it as stat tiles, a couple of bar charts (requests by status, queries by connection) and a per-connection table (queries, errors, average latency, rows) - a zero-setup live view for a deployment with no Prometheus/Grafana stack in front of it at all. It's deliberately a snapshot, not a dashboard: the numbers are this process's own totals since it started, with no history and no trends, the same limits above already describe. It reads /metrics as the administrator signed in to the Console, so it works with QUERYAPIGATE_METRICS_TOKEN set too; reading it again just re-fetches the current numbers - there's no polling or auto-refresh. For real history, trends and alerting, scrape /metrics with Prometheus and import documentation/grafana-dashboard.json into Grafana (Dashboards → New → Import, then upload the file or paste its contents) - it builds on exactly the metric names listed above, with panels for request/query rate and latency (p50/p95/p99), error rate, rows returned, active queries, pool occupancy and rate-limit rejections. Each QueryAPIGate process needs its own scrape target, and the dashboard sums across them.

h: Live events (Server-Sent Events) › GET /events on the main server

x: Since 0.25 (ADR 0012) each entry is a link in a hash chain: seq (1, 2, 3 ... across every instance, with no gaps), the previous entry's hash as its prev_hash, and its own hash over both and the entry. Change, remove, insert or reorder an entry, and every hash from there on stops matching. Keyed, or not. With QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY set (32 characters or more, kept outside the store like QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY), each hash is hmac-sha256:...: someone who can write to the store but hasn't the key can't re-sign an edit. Without it, sha256:... - consistent, but anyone with the store can recompute every hash after an edit; Settings says which is in effect. Setting a key is recorded (audit_key_set), and from then on an unkeyed entry - or a chain re-written unkeyed from the start - is a break. Rotating the key: QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY=, - the first signs, every one verifies; startup records audit_key_rotated. Keep the old key listed for as long as entries signed with it are kept. The rolling cap still applies: the chain's anchor remembers the newest entry trimmed, so the oldest kept must follow it - removing entries from the start isn't mistaken for a trim. With QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL set (the same value for both processes), a key's rate_limit of 100/minute is 100 calls a minute over REST and MCP together. Without it, each process counts on its own: 100 over REST and 100

t: MCP server
x: A tool call caps its result at QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_MAX_ROWS (default 200) rows, independent of QUERYAPIGATE_MAX_PAGE_SIZE - an LLM's context window can't hold a result the way a human paging through the admin UI can. A capped result says so: truncated is true, and it carries an agent-facing note ("…more rows match; add a filter, or ask for a summary with an aggregate") both as a field in structuredContent and as a second text block - so a model narrows the query or aggregates instead of assuming the rows it got are the whole answer. The first text block stays pure JSON. A caller-supplied page_size smaller than the cap is still honored.

x: What QueryAPIGate does, feature by feature, with links to the reference for each. The README has the short version; the API reference has every detail.

t: Features
x: Tier 1 - PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB and ClickHouse: every feature, tested against a real server in CI, and covered by the compatibility promise. Experimental - H2, generic JDBC (Oracle, SQL Server, DB2, Snowflake and anything else with a driver jar) and MongoDB (find() queries): they work, with documented gaps. The same guard, pooling, parameter binding and output formats - JSON, NDJSON, XML, YAML, CSV, TSV, Excel and Parquet - apply to every one. What each supports - read-only enforcement, time limits, allowed_tables, schema browsing, streaming - is in the support matrix. Files as a source - through DuckDB, Parquet, CSV and JSON files on local disk, S3, GCS, R2 or the web are queried where they are and published like any table, limited to the paths each connection lists (see publishing a bucket as an API).

t: Features
x: QueryAPIGate is built to expose specific query results, not database credentials: API key authentication, with hashed key storage (SHA-256, never the raw secret) in queryapigate.db. Database connection passwords encrypted at rest (QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY), decrypted only in memory at the moment a connection is opened; a literal password on disk is never returned to a client either way. Scoped API keys: restrict a key to a set of connections, and/or to a specific allow-list of saved queries, independent of any connection grant - individual queries in that list can also be curated for write access, without granting it anywhere else reachable through the key. Workspaces (experimental, ADR 0023): several teams on one server, each with its own connections, saved queries, API keys, roles, destinations and exports - names unique within it - and its own history, audit entries, alerts and events. An administrator can have a role in one workspace only; a workspace's owner manages its members. Every route also answers at /w//...; a key works in its own. Example APIs: queryapigate examples load installs four worked scenarios - a reporting API, dashboard data, a streaming export and a partner integration - as collections, queries, roles and a ready-to-use API key per scenario, touching nothing of yours, and removable again with one command. Collections: file saved queries into named groups

t: Features
x: A saved query bundles SQL, name, description, parameters, author, version, permissions and (optionally) cache configuration into one addressable resource: GET /q/. Saving again under the same name creates a new version rather than overwriting the old one, so a change to the SQL doesn't silently change what's already live; ?version=1 still runs the prior one, and each run is recorded in the query's execution history.

t: Features
x: SELECT * FROM film WHERE film_id = :id GET /q/film_by_id?id=7 Values are sent to the database separately from the SQL text, so they cannot be injected into it. Parameters can declare a type, default, required/optional, enum, numeric range, length and pattern - invalid input is rejected with a field-by-field 400 before it reaches the database.

t: Features
x: JSON, NDJSON, XML, YAML, CSV, TSV, XLSX and Parquet are all available per request (?format=), so the same saved query serves application clients, reporting and data pipelines - a Parquet export keeps column types and is typically a quarter of the CSV's size.

t: Features
x: ?page=2&page_size=50 pages results with X-Has-More telling the caller whether more exist. For full exports, ?stream=true&format=csv (or tsv/ndjson) streams the entire result straight from the database cursor rather than buffering it - verified end-to-end with 1,000,000-row results and flat server memory throughout (MySQL, PostgreSQL and ClickHouse); see Streaming exports for the measured numbers. queryapigate export --out '/exports/{name}_{date}.csv' wraps the same streaming path as a CLI command for cron/systemd/Kubernetes CronJob to call directly - no server needs to be running; see Scheduled exports to a file.

t: Features
x: Saved queries can opt into HTTP-level caching: cache_ttl, Cache-Control, ETag, conditional requests and 304 Not Modified, plus an X-Cache: HIT/MISS header. Never applied to a query that writes.

t: Features
x: A server-wide, IP-keyed limit (QUERYAPIGATE_RATE_LIMIT) and an independent, optional per-key limit can both be in effect at once - a request has to pass both. This lets different API consumers get different budgets: Internal dashboard -> generous server-wide limit, no per-key limit Partner key -> 200/hour of its own Trial key -> 20/hour of its own

t: Features

t: Features
x: Every call - REST, MCP, events or an export - passes the same eight stages, as the README's second diagram follows one through: Identify the caller - an API key, an admin token, a signed-in user's JWT or an OAuth token. Apply its limits - rate limit, IP allow-list, expiry. Check the grant - this query, this connection, read or write. Validate parameters - types, ranges, lengths; values are bound, never spliced into the SQL. Guard the SQL - one statement, read-only unless allowed, only the tables a key may see. Run it - on a pooled connection, within the caller's time and row limits. Mask and format - masking traced to the source columns, then the format asked for. Record it - run history, metrics and live events; the audit log for changes.

t: Threat model
x: SECURITY.md tells you what to do - a checklist to run through before a deployment goes live. This page explains why: what QueryAPIGate is actually defending against, how each defense works under the hood, and - just as importantly - where the defenses stop and become the operator's job instead. Read it before deciding QueryAPIGate is (or isn't) an appropriate way to expose a database to something you don't fully trust.

t: Threat model
x: QueryAPIGate sits between a caller and one or more real databases. Four things are worth protecting, in roughly descending order of damage if lost: The ability to execute arbitrary SQL/Mongo operations against a connected database - the whole point of the service, and therefore its biggest liability if it reaches the wrong caller. Database credentials - held in the store (queryapigate.db, or a PostgreSQL schema), needed to reach the databases at all. Query results and SQL text - a saved query's SQL, and the rows it returns, can themselves be sensitive (customer data, schema details, business logic) independent of write access. API key secrets and the audit trail - if either is compromised, every other control built on top of them (scoping, accountability) stops meaning anything.

t: Threat model
h: Who might attack it, and from where
x: An unauthenticated network attacker - anyone who can reach the HTTP port at all. The only thing standing between them and everything above is whether QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY is set (see Open-access mode below) and whether TLS is actually terminated somewhere in front of the service. A caller holding a scoped (non-admin) API key, acting maliciously or - more realistically - a legitimate integration whose key has leaked. The threat here isn't "can they authenticate," it's "how far can that one key's specific grants actually reach." An administrator - the holder of the shared QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY or of a named administrator's admin token - or anyone who steals one. What they can change depends on the role (below); but every role except auditor can run any SQL on every connection, so for the data each is equivalent to a database superuser scoped to whatever connections exist. This tier is not defended against by QueryAPIGate itself - see Non-goals. Someone with filesystem or volume access to QUERYAPIGATE_HOME - a compromised host, a misconfigured backup, a leaked volume snapshot. queryapigate.db is a single SQLite file holding connections, saved-query SQL, API key hashes, roles, execution history and the audit log - see Data at rest.

t: Threat model
Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Authentication: one shared secret, or many scoped ones
x: Every request carries (or omits) an X-API-Key header, checked once per request in app.py's before_request hook, before anything else runs. Two kinds of key exist: The admin key (QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY) is a single value living in the server's environment, compared with hmac.compare_digest (constant-time, so response timing can't be used to guess it character by character). It is never stored anywhere on disk - only in the process environment - and grants everything: every connection, every saved query, admin-only routes (managing connections, keys, roles). Admin tokens (qagadm_...) belong to named administrators (admins.py, ADR 0003): generated by the server, shown once, stored only as a SHA-256 hash and looked up by it, like scoped keys - but in their own table, and they authorize management by role rather than data access by grant. Each can carry an expiry; deactivating an administrator stops all of theirs at once. Scoped keys (POST /api/v1/api-keys, owners and admins to create) are generated by the server and shown exactly once - their secret is never stored, only a SHA-256 hash, in queryapigate.db's api_keys table. A lost scoped key cannot be recovered, only revoked and replaced, the same property a password reset flow gives you and a plaintext-stored secret never could. A key's secret can be reissued (ADR 0009, POST /api/v1/api-keys/{name}/rotate, access.write): the new one

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Authorization: what a scoped key can actually do
x: Three grant fields say what a key reaches, and they add up - a saved query is reachable if connections, collections or queries reaches it. The rest narrow what that reach may do, and none of them widens what another restricts: | Grant | Narrows | | connections | Which database connections ad-hoc SQL can target ("*" = all). | | collections | Which saved queries are reachable, by current collection membership - re-evaluated live, no wildcard. | | queries | Specific saved-query names reachable regardless of connection grants - the only way to give an external client curated access with no ad-hoc SQL capability at all. | | allow_writes | Whether write statements are permitted at all, on top of the server-wide QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES ceiling (a key can never grant itself more than the server allows). | | allowed_write_ops | Which specific write verbs (insert/update/delete/...) if writes are allowed. | | allowed_tables | Which tables a statement may touch - enforced via a real SQL parser (sqlglot), not a regex; unsupported for H2/JDBC connections, which are refused outright for a table-restricted key rather than silently under-checked. | | rate_limit | A per-key request budget, additive with the server-wide IP-based limit, never a way around it. | | expires_at | A day after which the key stops authenticating at all, checked live on every request. | | allowed_ips | Which source IPs/

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Administration: named administrators and roles
x: The Management API (/api/v1) is for administrators only. Every operation needs one capability, and each of four fixed roles holds a fixed set (adminroles.py), checked before any route runs; a test fails if an operation has no entry, so a new route can't ship unguarded. A scoped key or signed-in app user gets 403 admin_only; an administrator whose role lacks the capability, 403 role_forbidden. | Role | Can change | Data plane | | owner | everything, including administrators | any SQL, every connection | | admin | connections, API keys and roles, queries, cache - not administrators | any SQL, every connection | | developer | saved queries and collections | any SQL, every connection | | auditor | nothing - reads configuration, the audit log and history | none | What this buys, and what it doesn't: A stolen developer token can't mint keys, change connections or create administrators - but it can read every row on every connection. Roles bound management blast radius; for data, the database account behind each connection is still the backstop. Give someone a scoped API key instead when they need less data reach. Who can call what is an owner's or admin's decision. Moving a query into a collection, or merging collections, in a way that gives an API key or role new reach needs access.write, even for a role that may otherwise organise queries. A developer still decides what saved queri

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Workspaces: one team's reach, not another's (ADR 0023, experimental)
x: Workspaces (ADR 0023) let several teams administer one server: each owns its connections, saved queries, keys, roles, destinations and exports. The boundary they draw is between teams who share a server, not between a hosted service's tenants. What it holds against, and how: Every lookup is in one workspace. A request's workspace is settled once (app.settle_workspace(), kept on the request, never on a thread a later request reuses) and every statement on a workspace's table filters on it - names are unique per workspace in the store's own keys, so there is nothing for a forgotten filter to match by name alone across workspaces. Work that outlives the request - a stream's rows, queued history, events and usage counts carries the workspace it was started in. tests/test_workspace_isolation.py builds two workspaces with the same names for everything and checks each route reaches only its own: a lookup that forgot its workspace shows up there as the other workspace's data. A key can't leave its workspace, prefix or not: its secret says which workspace it is in. Naming another, or one that doesn't exist, is the same 404 - a caller can't use the error to list workspaces. A signed-in user can't leave their workspace either. A federated (JWT) user's workspace comes from the token - the QUERYAPIGATE_JWT_WORKSPACE_CLAIM claim, or the default workspace when that isn't configured - never fr

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Column masking: which values leave
x: A mask grant on a key, role or export (ADR 0005) hashes, masks, nulls or drops the values of named source columns in everything that caller receives. The design choice that matters: result columns are traced to their sources through the SQL (sqlglot lineage, by position, with the connection's schema for SELECT ), not matched by name - so SELECT email AS e, lower(email), a CTE or a UNION is still masked - and anything that can't be traced is refused before it runs, never served unmasked. Probing during the build found, and the tests now hold against, the ways tracing could be led astray: DuckDB's COLUMNS('regex') (columns picked by pattern), a table alias that renames columns (customer AS c(a, e)), SELECT over a NATURAL/USING join (fewer columns than parsed, which would shift every mask), whole-row references (row_to_json(c)), and a VALUES row holding a subquery. The database's error text, which can quote a value, is never returned to a caller with rules. The cache is keyed per set of rules, and run history records what was masked. What remains: Inference. A caller that writes SQL can filter and group on a masked column (WHERE email LIKE 'a%', GROUP BY email) - masking hides values in results, not answers about them. For callers near sensitive data, especially AI agents, grant saved queries only, or allowed_tables on a view that leaves the column out. Hashes show equality. hash

x: This is the part worth being the most precise about, because it's also the part with the sharpest edges. Bound :name parameters are real parameterization. sqltools.bind_parameters() rewrites :name into the target driver's native paramstyle and hands values to the driver separately from the SQL text - the same mechanism that makes parameterized queries safe in any language. x: A trino connection reaches every catalog the Trino cluster federates - Hive, Iceberg, Kafka, other databases - through one QueryAPIGate connection. Reviewed for its introduction (experimental, ADR 0026): allowed_tables is matched fully qualified (catalog.schema.table), not by bare name. So a grant of orders reaches only the default catalog+schema's orders - never orders in another catalog or schema - and hive.sales.orders reaches exactly that table. (a pass-through that would run arbitrary SQL on a backend), table_changes(...) - names no base table the allow-list can account for, so a table-restricted key is refused (table_not_allowed), as read_parquet()/url() are on other dialects. t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Secrets at rest
x: Connection passwords in the store can be a literal string, an "${ENV_VAR}" reference resolved from the process environment at load time (never written back to disk), or - with QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY set - Fernet-encrypted at rest. Encryption is opt-in, not the default; without a secret key, a connection password is only as protected as the file/volume it sits in. The key itself must be kept outside QUERYAPIGATE_HOME and out of version control - there is no recovery path for an encrypted password without it, by design, the same property that makes it real encryption rather than obfuscation. API responses always mask stored passwords regardless of how they're stored. The key can be rotated without taking a connection down (ADR 0009): QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY lists the new key first and the old one after it, queryapigate rekey re-encrypts every stored password under the new one in a single transaction (all or nothing), and the old key is then removed. A key suspected leaked is replaced the same way; backups taken before the rekey still open with the old key, so they need retiring with it.

t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › The audit trail
x: The audit log is a hash chain (ADR 0012): each entry's hash covers the previous entry's, so changing, removing, inserting or reordering one breaks every hash after it, and queryapigate audit verify (and a check every 5 minutes) names the first. Against someone who can write to the store, a plain hash is only consistency - they can recompute it - so with QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY set the chain is HMAC-signed with a key kept outside the store, and a key once set means every newer entry must carry it. What the chain can't show alone: the newest entries deleted (its end can't know what came after it), and a rewrite by someone holding both the store and the key. Both are why a copy outside - the SIEM stream, or the export file shipped elsewhere - matters. The stream sends each entry with its seq and hash over TLS - the server's certificate verified, the client's optional - so a later rewrite of the store contradicts what the SIEM already has; its delivery is at least once, and syslog over TCP can lose the batch sent to a SIEM that dies without closing the connection (OTLP, acknowledged per batch, doesn't). queryapigate audit verify --file checks the SIEM's copy on its own - repeats from at-least-once delivery dropped only when exact. x: QueryAPIGate does not terminate TLS itself - that is explicitly the reverse proxy's job (Caddy, nginx, Traefik; see DEPLOYMENT.md). An API key travels in a request header, so serving over plain HTTP means the key is recoverable by anyone who can observe the traffic - TLS termination in front of QueryAPIGate is not optional once a key exists. Response headers don't depend on that proxy (ADR 0010): every response sets nosniff, Cache-Control: no-store (a cached saved query private, never shareable: callers authenticate with X-API-Key, which HTTP's shared-cache rule doesn't cover - the 0.22.1 fix) and, on API responses, a CSP that runs nothing and a no-referrer policy. x: Where data goes is the inventory; what bears on threats: Values stay out of what's kept by default. h: Security architecture, by control › Live events (ADR 0020)
x: GET /events - on the main server, and queryapigate events for many clients - streams each run as it happens: which query, on which connection, by which key, how it went, and an ad-hoc run's SQL as history keeps it. So: Never public. A real key or a signed-in user's token, in a header - never the URL, where it would reach access logs - unless the server runs with no keys at all. A stream is checked again every minute, so a revoked key or an expired token loses it within about a minute and a quarter. The admin key and data administrators see every run; anyone else only their own - the runs made with that key, or by that user, since the key was created. Filters only narrow that, and their values are bound, never SQL. Key names can't hold the : of jwt:, and an administrator's name can't be a key's. Not bounded: how many of those streams one key holds. Kept for a while, and forgettable: the event log keeps QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_RETENTION_HOURS (24 by default), and history forget erases a caller's events with their runs. Reviewed for 0.34 (ADR 0021). t: Threat model
h: Security architecture, by control › Rate limiting and abuse prevention
x: The rate limiter throttles both by source IP (server-wide) and, additively, by API key (rate_limit grant). Without QUERYAPIGATE_REDIS_URL its state is in each process's memory, so running more than one process silently multiplies the effective limit. With it, every instance and process counts against one budget in Redis (an atomic token bucket, on Redis's own clock); if Redis becomes unreachable, each process falls back to its own counting - limits stay enforced, per process, never lifted - and the rate_limits_not_shared alert and a metric say so. QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY tells the server how many reverse-proxy hops to trust when resolving the real client IP from X-Forwarded-For - left at its default of 0 with a direct-connecting client, or set to the actual hop count behind a proxy; getting this wrong in either direction lets a client forge its apparent IP and evade both the rate limiter and allowed_ips checks. A rate limit counts calls, not what they cost, so a key under its rate can still hold every pooled connection with slow queries and starve everyone sharing them. A key's or role's own max_concurrent, query_timeout and max_rows (ADR 0011) bound that: queries running at once (a stream counts until its last row), how long each may run, how many rows a call returns - each only ever narrowing the server's limits. t: Security policy
x: Releases meet SLSA Build Level 2: each artifact is built on a GitHub-hosted runner by a workflow in this repository, and comes with provenance - which workflow, at which commit, from which tag - that the build platform signs (GitHub artifact attestations, through Sigstore), so it can't be forged without that workflow. That holds for: the images and the Helm chart, from 0.31 (docker.yml); the sdist and wheel on PyPI, from 0.35.1 (release.yml). Earlier ones carry only PyPI's own attestations (PEP 740), which say who uploaded them, not how they were built. To check one: bash pip download queryapigate==0.35.1 --no-deps -d . gh attestation verify queryapigate-0.35.1-py3-none-any.whl --owner AnanthaRajuC Not Level 3. Level 3 asks that the steps doing the build can't influence the provenance. Here the attestation is made in the same job as the build, so a compromised build step - a poisoned dependency of the build, say - could in principle shape what gets attested. Building and attesting in a reusable workflow, isolated from the caller, is the documented way to Level 3; it isn't done yet.

x: Set QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY, and put the service behind TLS (a reverse proxy) - the key is sent in a header. It is the shared, full-access admin key; give anyone or anything that only needs to run queries a scoped key instead (POST /api/v1/api-keys), limited to specific connections and, separately, to read-only access. Give the people (and pipelines) who manage the server their own admin tokens, with the narrowest role that fits - queryapigate admins create NAME --role owner for the first - and then keep the shared key sealed as a break-glass key, or remove it (guide 43). Leave QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES unset unless you really need writes, and connect with a database account that only has the privileges the API should have. The read-only guard - including the single-statement check it relies on - is defence in depth, not a substitute for grants; it is dialect-aware (MySQL/ClickHouse honour backslash escapes in string literals by default, PostgreSQL/SQLite/H2 do not) and is exercised by a fuzz test suite (tests/test_sql_guard_fuzz.py), but a regex-based guard can never be a full SQL parser for every server mode. t: Architecture overview
h: 1. What it is, and the trust boundary
x: QueryAPIGate is a self-hosted gateway, open source under Apache-2.0. It turns saved SQL queries into REST endpoints, MCP tools for AI agents, live server-sent events and exports. A saved query is versioned, and its parameters are typed and bound to the driver rather than written into the SQL. Every call goes through one governed path: authentication, limits, grants, a SQL guard, masking and a run-history record. It is a Python (Flask) application. The admin UI, the Console, is a React single-page app that ships inside the same package. Trust boundary. QueryAPIGate runs inside the customer's network, on infrastructure the customer operates. No part of it is a hosted service. It connects outward only to systems the deployer configures: the databases and file locations that connections name; its own metadata store (SQLite or PostgreSQL) and, optionally, Redis; an identity provider, for Console sign-in, signed-in app users and MCP clients; secret providers: files, HashiCorp Vault, and AWS (experimental); export destinations (object-storage buckets or allowed local folders); a SIEM, an OpenTelemetry collector and a Prometheus scraper. QueryAPIGate does not terminate TLS. A reverse proxy or ingress in front of it does that, and is required once any key exists. QueryAPIGate is not a network perimeter or a web application firewall: network policy, a VPN or a proxy still decides who can

x: Every front door applies the same governance code (authentication, rate limits, metrics). A saved-query call then passes eight steps. This is a model of what is checked, not a strict order: the server-wide rate limit applies before the key is checked, and a column masking can't trace is refused before the query runs. Codes are from the API.md error catalogue; code is under the compatibility promise. Identify the caller. Admin key or scoped key (X-API-Key; the admin key compared in constant time, scoped keys looked up by SHA-256 hash), an administrator's token, a JWT (Authorization: Bearer), or on MCP an OAuth access token. Fails 401 unauthorized; on MCP, a token without the configured scope is 403 insufficient_scope. Apply its limits. Server-wide per-address and per-key rate limits (429 rate_limited), usage quotas, checked before the response cache (429 quota_exceeded), max_concurrent (429 too_many_concurrent). allowed_ips and expires_at fail like a wrong key (401 unauthorized), so the caller learns nothing about why. Check the grant. The key's connections, collections or queries grant must reach the query or connection: 403 connection_forbidden or 403 forbidden; 403 connection_inactive; 404 query_not_found or 404 not_published. On the Management API: 403 admin_only or 403 role_forbidden. Validate parameters. Each value is checked against its declared type and rules, then bound

t: Architecture overview
x: Administrators: four fixed roles (owner, admin, developer, auditor), personal admin tokens stored as hashes with optional expiry. The shared QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY remains a break-glass owner key; once a named owner exists, each use is audited and alerted. Console SSO (OIDC): authorization code flow with PKCE (S256) as a confidential client, so the browser never holds a token. State, nonce and verifier are server-side, single-use, valid ten minutes; the ID token's signature, issuer, audience, azp, nonce and expiry are checked. People are bound by sub; roles come from IdP groups at each sign-in. Session cookie Host-, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict, stored as a hash, paired with a CSRF token. QUERYAPIGATE_SSO_ONLY removes personal tokens from SSO users. Tested against Keycloak 26. App users (JWT/JWKS): RS256 against a JWKS, or HS256 with a shared secret. exp required; iss/aud enforced (mandatory with a JWKS); HMAC and public-key families can't be mixed; none never accepted. Grants come from a role, read live. A JWT can't be revoked before it expires. MCP clients (OAuth 2.1): the MCP server is a resource server. A token's aud must be the MCP server's URL and it must carry the configured scope; the algorithm comes from the provider's published key, never the token header; provider metadata is fetched over https:// only and must name the configured issuer (RFC 8414). t: Architecture overview
x: From 0.31, every image (both variants, multi-arch) and the Helm chart is signed keyless with cosign, by digest, by the repository's docker.yml release workflow on the release tag. The signature is recorded in Sigstore's public log. Each release is signed in two forms: the Sigstore bundle and the classic .sig tag, which admission controllers need. Releases before 0.31 are not signed. Provenance and SBOM: images carry SLSA provenance, an SPDX SBOM and a GitHub artifact attestation naming the commit; the chart has a GitHub attestation; PyPI releases use trusted publishing, with PEP 740 attestations. Pinned builds: base images are pinned by digest; every GitHub Action is pinned by commit SHA, and a test refuses a uses: without one; downloaded tools are checked against their published checksums; Dependabot proposes updates as reviewed commits. Verifying: cosign verify with the workflow identity and the GitHub OIDC issuer, gh attestation verify, the SBOM, and an admission policy that admits only signed images. Sigstore policy-controller and Kyverno are covered. Guide 59 walks through each one. SECURITY.md has the summary. A signature shows which workflow and tag built a release. It does not show that the code is correct, and builds are not reproducible byte for byte (ADR 0018).

x: These are answers to the questions a vendor security questionnaire (SIG Lite, CAIQ, or a customer's own) usually asks, for QueryAPIGate 0.40.0. QueryAPIGate is a self-hosted, open source (Apache-2.0) gateway that turns saved SQL into governed REST, MCP, event and export endpoints. How to read them: The answers describe the software: what it does, what it stores, and where its controls stop. QueryAPIGate runs inside your environment, so the answers about your deployment (which features are on, who operates it, how the host and network are secured) are yours to give. In this document, "Deployer" means you, the customer running QueryAPIGate. Items marked Deployer: name a control that is your responsibility, or that depends on how you configure it. Each answer cites its source. Files in this pack sit side by side (THREAT_MODEL.md, DATA_PROTECTION.md, SECURITY.md, DEPLOYMENT.md, ARCHITECTURE.md). Other sources are linked in the project's repository. Where a source didn't support a claim, the claim was left out. To check the answers against your own running server, see guide 57.

x: What access-control model does the product use? Answer: Administrators have one of four fixed roles, each holding a fixed set of capabilities: owner: everything; admin: everything except administrators; developer: saved queries and collections; auditor: read-only, with no SQL. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#administration-named-administrators-and-roles What can a scoped API key be restricted to? The other fields only ever narrow that reach. A queries grant alone gives an external client curated access to named saved queries, with no ad-hoc SQL at all. x: What customer data does the product store? Answer: The store holds configuration (connections, saved queries and their versions, keys, roles and administrators), run history, usage counters, the event log, the audit log, and an agent's write requests. Query results are not stored, except by the response cache and exports when the Deployer turns them on. Parameter values are not stored either: run history records parameter names, never their values. Answer: The product processes: callers' names, which for a signed-in user is jwt:, often an email address; administrators' names and email addresses; IP addresses; an AI agent's write arguments; whatever the connected databases hold, which passes through. With no SSO and no JWTs, no person is named, only API keys. Source: DATA_PROTECTION.md#personal-data-it-handles, guide 57 Is personal data written to logs? Some things can still reach the log: an ad-hoc statement's text, and a database's own error message, which can quote a value. This is opt-in, not the default. API keys, admin tokens and session ids are stored only as SHA-256 hashes. The rest of the store (configuration and run history) is not encrypted by QueryAPIGate. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#secrets-at-rest, DATA_PROTECTION.md#cryptography, guide 57 Can database credentials be kept out of the product's store entirely? Answer: Yes. A password can be a reference: ${VAR}, ${file:...} or ${vault:...}, or short-lived Vault database credentials. References to AWS Secrets Manager and RDS IAM are experimental. Resolved values are held only in memory and never written to the store, a log, a response, a trace or the audit log. Nothing is reachable through a reference until the Deployer allow-lists it. t: Security questionnaire answers
x: Are administrative actions logged? Answer: Yes. Every configuration change is appended to the audit log, recording: the actor; how they authenticated (via: their own token, break-glass key, SSO, CLI, configuration file); the action and target; a diff of what changed. Passwords appear only as or "changed", and secrets and hashes never appear. Every SSO sign-in, refusal and sign-out is recorded. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#audit-logging-and-data-at-rest, API.md, Audit log Is the audit log tamper-evident? Answer: Yes. It is a hash chain, HMAC-signed when QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY is set. Changing, removing, inserting or reordering an entry breaks the chain, which queryapigate audit verify detects; a check runs every 5 minutes and raises the critical audit_chain_broken alert. The chain alone can't show that its newest entries were deleted, or that someone holding both the store and the key rewrote it. A copy kept outside the store is what proves those. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#the-audit-trail Can audit logs be sent to a SIEM? Answer: Yes. The audit log can be sent as syslog over TLS (RFC 5425), with optional mutual TLS, or as OTLP logs. Each entry carries its seq and hash, and audit verify --file checks the SIEM's copy. Delivery is at least once and survives the SIEM being down. Syslog over TCP can lose a batch if the receiver dies without closing the connection; OTLP acknowledges each bat

t: Security questionnaire answers
x: Does the product support high availability? Answer: Yes, with several instances on a PostgreSQL store with Redis. Everything is then shared, so instances are interchangeable behind a load balancer. This is tested in CI with three real servers. With a SQLite store, only one instance is supported; two replicas with their own SQLite volumes are two separate servers. Without Redis, rate limits and the cache are per process, and the instances_not_shared alert reports it. If Redis becomes unreachable, rate limits stay enforced per process, never lifted, and the rate_limits_not_shared alert says so. Source: DEPLOYMENT.md#scaling-out, THREAT_MODEL.md#non-goals-what-this-does-not-defend-against How is the product's data backed up and restored? Answer: A SQLite store is backed up with queryapigate backup, which uses SQLite's backup API to take a consistent copy while the server runs. A PostgreSQL store is backed up with pg_dump, or the database's own backups. CI backs up a store, loses it, restores it, and checks the result on every run. Deployer: schedule backups, ship them off the host, and test restores. Source: DEPLOYMENT.md#5-persistent-data-backups-and-restores What does a backup not contain? Answer: A backup doesn't contain: QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY, without which encrypted passwords are unreadable; the admin key; environment variables that connections reference; the connected data

t: Security questionnaire answers
x: Does the product set HTTP security headers? Answer: Yes. Every response sets X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Cache-Control: no-store; a cached saved query is private. API responses also carry a CSP that allows nothing and Referrer-Policy: no-referrer. The server version banner is removed. HSTS is opt-in (QUERYAPIGATE_HSTS_MAX_AGE) and sent only over HTTPS. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#transport, ADR 0010 How is TLS provided? Answer: By a reverse proxy the Deployer runs (Caddy, nginx or Traefik). QueryAPIGate does not terminate TLS itself. Deployer: terminate TLS in front of the server, and set QUERYAPIGATE_TRUST_PROXY to the number of proxy hops. Leave it at 0 when clients connect directly. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#transport, DEPLOYMENT.md#2-compose-file, SECURITY.md#hardening-checklist-for-deployments Is cross-origin (CORS) access restricted? Answer: Yes. CORS is off unless QUERYAPIGATE_CORS_ORIGINS is set, and cookies are not used for API credentials. CORS controls browsers only; it is not authentication. Deployer: list only sites you control, and never use * without an API key. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#cors, API.md, Rate limiting and CORS Does the container run as a non-root user? Answer: Yes. The image runs as a non-root user (UID 1000) and ships a HEALTHCHECK. Source: DEPLOYMENT.md#1-the-image What pod security does the Helm chart apply? Answer: The chart's pods run as UID 10

t: Security questionnaire answers
x: What does the product explicitly not defend against? Answer: QueryAPIGate does not defend against: network attacks: it is not a network perimeter or a web application firewall; a malicious administrator: an owner, admin or developer can read every row on every connection; a missed statement: the read-only guard doesn't replace least-privilege database credentials; planted instructions: an AI agent may be steered by what it reads. The threat model lists the rest. Run history isn't tamper-evident, connection metadata is visible to every administrator, query names can be probed, and /metrics is open until a token is set. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#non-goals-what-this-does-not-defend-against What are the limits of the read-only SQL guard? Answer: It is a regex-based classifier, not a SQL parser. It is dialect-aware and fuzz-tested, but it can never be a full parser for every server mode. On DuckDB, H2 and JDBC connections, which are opened read-write, the guard is the only lock against writes. The project assumes it could have another gap like the one already found and fixed. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#query-execution-what-actually-stops-a-bad-statement, SECURITY.md#hardening-checklist-for-deployments Are query time limits enforced on every connection type? Answer: No. On generic JDBC connections, QUERYAPIGATE_QUERY_TIMEOUT is not enforced, because JDBC has no portable way to cancel a st

t: Security questionnaire answers
x: Do you hold a SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certification? Answer: No. SOC 2 and ISO 27001 assess an organisation running a service. QueryAPIGate is software that runs inside the Deployer's environment, under the Deployer's controls, so there is no hosted service to certify. What it provides is the evidence your own assessment needs: this pack, the threat model, the data inventory and checks you can run on your own server. Deployer: your own SOC 2 or ISO 27001 scope covers how you run QueryAPIGate: hosts, network, secrets, backups, access reviews and log retention. Source: guide 57 Has the product undergone an independent third-party penetration test or audit? Answer: The project publishes no third-party penetration test or audit report. Its own security reviews are recorded in the threat model, feature by feature, with what each looked at and what it found. Source: THREAT_MODEL.md#console-sign-in-through-sso-adr-0007 (an example review record), ADR 0017
