t: Run several instances behind a load balancer
x: The reference deployment is in the repository, under deploy/scale-out/: three instances, PostgreSQL, Redis, the events server and Caddy in front. cd deploy/scale-out cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env # pin QUERYAPIGATE_IMAGE; set the key, passwords and SITE_ADDRESS docker compose up -d docker compose ps # six services, healthy curl https://api.example.com/health Caddy round-robins requests across the three instances, checks each one's /health, takes a failing one out of the rotation, and retries a request on another instance if one can't be reached. /events goes to the events server, and /metrics is blocked at the proxy (scrape the instances directly).

t: Run several instances behind a load balancer
x: deploy/kubernetes/ has a Deployment of three replicas, the events server, Services, a PodDisruptionBudget and an Ingress (ingress-nginx; adapt the annotations for another controller): cp secret.example.yaml secret.yaml # fill in - or create the Secret from your secret manager kubectl apply -f secret.yaml -f queryapigate.yaml kubectl rollout status deploy/queryapigate Use a managed PostgreSQL and Redis in production; dev-dependencies.yaml starts throwaway ones for trying it. Settings in the manifest that matter, each found by running it: enableServiceLinks: false. Kubernetes puts _PORT=tcp://... into every pod for each Service, so a Service named queryapigate-events sets QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_PORT - one of QueryAPIGate's own settings. The first deployment of these manifests crashed on exactly that. QueryAPIGate now ignores such a value with a warning naming the cause, and the manifest switches service links off. A preStop pause and a 45-second grace period. Without them, a rolling update dropped requests that arrived while a pod was being removed - 2 of 1,633 in the test. With them: 1 of 1,805 in one run (a timeout) and 0 of 1,896 in another. maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1. Replace one pod at a time - the previous release keeps serving on the upgraded store meanwhile. Readiness and liveness probes on /health. A pod gets traffic only once it answers.

t: Give your team their own admin access
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: everyone who manages QueryAPIGate signing in as themselves, with a role that fits what they do; CI on a token of its own; an audit log that says who changed what; and the shared QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY retired to a break-glass key - or removed. Until now, managing the server meant holding QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY: everyone could do everything, and the audit log said admin for every change. Named administrators change that (ADR 0003). Data callers - scoped API keys, signed-in app users - aren't affected. Every command and response below was run against a real server.

x: On the machine (or in the container) where the store is - no running server and no key needed: queryapigate admins create alice --role owner --email alice@corp.com --label laptop Created administrator alice (owner). Admin token tok_7c663440dc14 for alice (expires 2027-01-03) - store it now, it cannot be shown again: qagadm_9-2fLdbDffa6PaOdzKttS2U6j01oA9DiUoCawF3i8CE Use it as the X-API-Key header, or paste it into the Console's key box. t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: a saved query delivered every day as a Parquet file to a bucket your partner reads from - only the rows that are new since the last delivery, with every run on record, an alert when one fails, and nothing ever written outside the prefix you allowed. Every command and response below was run against a real server and an S3-compatible bucket (SeaweedFS), with the example APIs loaded. $TOKEN is an owner's or admin's admin token (the shared key works too).

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
h: Step 1: A query that can say "only what's new"
x: An incremental export remembers the largest value of one column it has delivered - the watermark - and binds it to a parameter on the next run. So the query needs a column that only grows, and a parameter to compare it with: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "rentals_after", "connection_name": "examples", "description": "Rentals after an id", "publish": true, "sql": "SELECT rental_id, rental_date, amount FROM rental WHERE rental_id > :after ORDER BY rental_id", "parameters": {"after": {"type": "int", "min": 0}} }' Pick the column with care. An id that only grows (rental_id) is the safest: nothing is missed and nothing is sent twice. A timestamp (updated_at > :since) works too, but > can miss a row written later with the same timestamp as the last one delivered, and >= re-sends the rows on the boundary. And the parameter must accept what the column holds: a date-only parameter can't take a timestamp watermark - the run says so, and writes nothing.

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
h: Step 2: The destination - where it may write, and nowhere else
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/destinations -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "acme", "url": "s3://acme-exchange/from-us/", "user": "AKIA...", "password": "${ACME_SECRET_KEY}", "region": "eu-west-1" }' url is the prefix exports may write under: s3://, gs:// (with "storage": "gcs" HMAC keys), r2:// (with account_id), or a local folder - which must sit inside one the operator set in QUERYAPIGATE_EXPORT_DIRS, never the server's own home. For an S3-compatible service, add endpoint, "url_style": "path" and "use_ssl": false without TLS. The secret is stored like a connection password: here a ${ACME_SECRET_KEY} reference to the server's environment; a typed one is masked in every response and encrypted with QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY. Nothing can be written outside the prefix. Every write goes through a DuckDB connection locked to it - no path, parameter or file name can reach s3://acme-exchange/other-partner/; DuckDB refuses. Still give the credentials write access to that prefix only: two locks. Test it before anything depends on it - it writes one small file, _queryapigate_probe.csv, overwritten each time: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/destinations/acme/test -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" # {"object": "s3://acme-exchange/from-us/_queryapigate_probe.csv", "elapsed_ms": 251.0} In the Console: Delivery → Destinations → New destination

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/exports -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "acme-rentals", "query": "rentals_after", "destination": "acme", "path": "rentals/{date}/rentals_{run}.parquet", "incremental": {"column": "rental_id", "parameter": "after", "start": 0} }' path is under the destination. {date} (YYYY-MM-DD), {time}, {run} (the run's id - every file unique), {name} and the query's parameters ({region}, plain values only) are filled in. format: parquet (default), csv or ndjson, written by DuckDB with the rows in the query's order. A Parquet file keeps the column types - decimals exact, dates as dates. It's checked now, not at 3 a.m.: the destination and the published query must exist, the query must use :after, every placeholder must fill in.

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/exports/acme-rentals/runs -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" {"id": "ec7e7e7e8cb5", "export": "acme-rentals", "rows": 20000, "object": "s3://acme-exchange/from-us/rentals/2026-10-09/rentals_ec7e7e7e8cb5.parquet", "watermark": {"from": null, "to": 20000}, "duration_ms": 100.7} Run again straight away, and there is nothing new - so no file (skip_empty, on by default): {"id": "3ef429ef0f03", "rows": 0, "object": null, "watermark": {"from": 20000, "to": 20000}} Three new rentals later, the next run delivers exactly those: {"id": "622ec9e44786", "rows": 3, "object": "s3://acme-exchange/from-us/rentals/2026-10-09/rentals_622ec9e44786.parquet", "watermark": {"from": 20000, "to": 20003}} In the Console: Delivery → Exports → Run now, and Runs for its history.

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
h: Step 5: Put it on a schedule
x: QueryAPIGate doesn't keep a clock; your scheduler calls it. From the server's own host - no server needed, it reads the store directly: # crontab: every day at 06:00 0 6 * * * QUERYAPIGATE_HOME=/srv/queryapigate ACME_SECRET_KEY=... queryapigate exports run acme-rentals # Wrote 3 rows to s3://acme-exchange/from-us/rentals/2026-10-09/rentals_622ec9e44786.parquet (run 622ec9e44786). # Watermark: 20000 -> 20003 Or over HTTP, from a Kubernetes CronJob or Airflow, with a token of its own - a developer may run exports, but not define or change them: apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: CronJob metadata: name: acme-rentals spec: schedule: "0 6 * * *" concurrencyPolicy: Forbid jobTemplate: spec: backoffLimit: 2 template: spec: restartPolicy: Never containers: name: run image: curlimages/curl:8.10.1 args: ["-fsS", "-X", "POST", "-H", "X-API-Key: $(QUERYAPIGATE_TOKEN)", "http://queryapigate:5000/api/v1/exports/acme-rentals/runs"] env: name: QUERYAPIGATE_TOKEN valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: queryapigate-ci, key: token}} -f makes a failed run fail the job, so Kubernetes retries it and reports it. Two runs of one export never overlap, whoever starts them: the second answers 409 export_running (with Retry-After) until the first finishes - and a run that crashed holds the export only until its lease expires.

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
x: With the bucket unreachable: {"error": "Couldn't write s3://acme-exchange/from-us/rentals/2026-10-09/rentals_a55563feae35.parquet: IO Error: Could not connect to server ...", "code": "destination_unreachable"} Nothing is lost. The watermark moves only after a file is written, so it stayed at 20003. When the bucket was back, the next run delivered the one waiting row - {"rows": 1, "watermark": {"from": 20003, "to": 20004}}. An object store upload is all or nothing: a failed run leaves no partial file. You're told. The export_failing alert - Export 'acme-rentals' is failing - is on the Alerts screen and GET /api/v1/alerts until a run succeeds, and every run, failed or not, is in GET /api/v1/exports/acme-rentals/runs and run history, with who ran it. Re-send on purpose by moving the watermark back - audited: PATCH /api/v1/exports/acme-rentals with {"watermark": 19000}, or {"watermark": null} to start again from start.

t: Deliver a daily file to a partner's bucket
x: Memory. A run streams the rows through the server once, into a temporary file, and DuckDB writes from it: about 150 MB for a local file whatever the size, and 180-300 MB to S3 for 2-6 million rows (measured; the S3 upload's parts grow a little with the file). Who may do what. Owners and admins define destinations and exports - that decides who receives data. Developers may run them; auditors may read them. Scoped API keys can't touch them. What's in the files is what the query returns. To hide columns from a partner - email addresses, say - give the export masking rules. One-off files, without saving an export: queryapigate export rentals_after --param after=0 --to acme --format csv --out 'adhoc/{date}.csv'.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: one saved query - or a connection a partner or an AI agent may write SQL against - where the email addresses come back as stable codes and names as I*, whatever the SQL calls the columns; queries that masking can't follow refused rather than served; and a record of what was masked, for whom. Every command and response below was run against a real server with the example APIs loaded (demo-key is an admin).

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
h: Step 1: Give the caller its rules
x: Masking rules most often belong to the caller - an API key, a role (and so the keys made from it and the signed-in users mapped to it), or an export - so one saved query serves your own team as it is and a partner masked. A rule can also belong to the query itself, when a column should be masked for everyone who runs it, admins included - see Step 6. curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/api-keys -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "acme-partner", "connections": ["examples"], "mask": [{"column": "customer.email", "action": "hash"}, {"column": "customer.last_name", "action": "mask"}] }' A rule names a source column - table.column, or schema.table.column, with * as a wildcard (*.email, customer._name) - and what to do with its values: | Action | Turns isla.ito1@example.com into | When | | hash | eafbbd68098fdc3c | the same value always gives the same code, so counting, grouping and joining still work | | mask | i@example.com (text: Ito -> I*) | people should see there is a value, not what it is | | null | null | the column should stay, empty | | drop | (column removed) | it shouldn't appear at all | | keep | (unchanged) | to say a column is fine as it is - see views, below | The strictest rule that applies wins (drop > null > mask > hash). In the Console: API keys → New API key → Column masking; keys and roles with rules carry a masked t

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
x: The same saved query, for the admin and for the partner: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/customer_contacts -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # [{"customer_id": 1, "first_name": "Isla", "last_name": "Ito", "contact": "isla.ito1@example.com"}, ...] curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/customer_contacts -H 'X-API-Key: ' # [{"customer_id": 1, "first_name": "Isla", "last_name": "I*", "contact": "eafbbd68098fdc3c"}, # {"customer_id": 2, "first_name": "Ava", "last_name": "I*", "contact": "4b3ca6ce45e20366"}, ...] The query calls the column contact, not email - it's still hashed, because rules follow the data, not the name. The same goes for every format (?format=csv, Parquet), ?stream=true exports, MCP tools and the cache: a partner is never served a response cached for someone else. The caller can see what it gets masked, in GET /catalog: {"name": "customer_contacts", "masking": {"masked": [{"column": "last_name", "action": "mask"}, {"column": "contact", "action": "hash"}], "refused": null}}

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
h: Step 3: Let them write SQL - masking holds
x: A partner, or an AI agent over MCP, with the connection in its grant can write its own SQL. Each result column is traced through the SQL to the table columns it's computed from, so renaming, wrapping or nesting doesn't get the value out: # SELECT email FROM customer LIMIT 2 [{"email": "eafbbd68098fdc3c"}, {"email": "4b3ca6ce45e20366"}] # SELECT upper(email) AS e FROM customer LIMIT 2 - computed from email: hashed as a whole [{"e": "f94742444fd906a6"}, {"e": "b313c006e2be7cad"}] # WITH x AS (SELECT email AS e FROM customer) SELECT e AS anything FROM x LIMIT 2 [{"anything": "eafbbd68098fdc3c"}, {"anything": "4b3ca6ce45e20366"}] A query masking can't follow is refused - before it runs - rather than served unmasked: # SELECT c FROM customer c - the whole row as one value {"error": "This query's result columns can't be traced to their sources for masking: Column '\"c\"' could not be resolved", "code": "mask_unresolvable"} Refused the same way: table functions (read_parquet(...)), a table alias that renames columns (customer AS c(a, e)), SELECT * over a NATURAL or USING join, LATERAL, recursive CTEs, DuckDB's COLUMNS('...'), and functions masking can't see into (version()) - name the columns instead. A caller with rules also never sees the database's own error text, which can quote a value.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
x: Every run records what was masked, in run history: {"key_name": "acme-partner", "masked": [{"column": "email", "action": "hash", "source": "customer.email"}], ...} So "was the email ever returned unmasked to this partner?" is a search in GET /api/v1/history?key=acme-partner.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
h: Step 5: Files for the partner, masked too
x: An export carries its own rules, whoever runs it (deliver a daily file): curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/exports -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "acme-contacts", "query": "customer_contacts", "destination": "acme-drop", "format": "csv", "path": "contacts/{date}.csv", "mask": [{"column": "customer.email", "action": "hash"}, {"column": "customer.last_name", "action": "drop"}] }' customer_id,first_name,contact 1,Isla,eafbbd68098fdc3c 2,Ava,4b3ca6ce45e20366 The codes match the partner's API key's: one hash key per store, so a partner can join a file to an API response on them. Masking an export's incremental column is refused - the watermark is made of its values.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
h: Step 6: Or mask a column for everyone, on the query
x: When a column should never leave a particular query unmasked - no matter who calls it, admins included - put the rule on the query rather than on each caller. In the Console it's the Column masking field on the save form (API Repository → New version, or the API Designer's Save as New API); the same field in the Designer's Settings pane masks a preview before you save. In a query definition it's a mask array, the same shape as a caller's: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "customer_contacts", "connection_name": "examples", "sql": "SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email AS contact FROM customer", "mask": [{"column": "customer.email", "action": "hash"}] }' Now everyone who runs customer_contacts gets contact hashed, including demo-key. A caller that also carries a mask on its key gets both: per column, the stricter action wins (drop > null > mask > hash), so a query's hash and a key's drop on the same column drops it. Query-level masking traces SQL columns the same way, so it's not available on Mongo queries, and a query whose mask can't be traced is refused rather than served unmasked - exactly as for a caller's rules.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
x: Asking about a value without selecting it. A caller that writes SQL can still filter and group on a masked column: # SELECT count(*) AS n FROM customer WHERE email LIKE 'a%' [{"n": 15}] Masking hides values in what comes back; it doesn't stop a question about them. When that matters - an AI agent near sensitive data - give the caller saved queries only (no connections grant), or allowed_tables on a view that leaves the column out. Hashes are keyed, so a likely value can't be hashed and compared - but equal values are visible as equal, which is the point of hash.

t: Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent
x: Views are traced only as far as the view. A rule on customer.email can't tell whether contact_view.email is that column, so a query reading it is refused until a rule names the view: *.email (which covers every table and view), contact_view.email with an action, or contact_view.email with keep to say it's fine. Window functions are masked when they order or partition by a masked column - RANK() OVER (ORDER BY email) comes back hashed. Over other columns they're fine. Administrators see data as it is - masking is for the callers you hand data to. Auditors see no data at all. The hash key is made once per store and shared by every instance; set QUERYAPIGATE_MASK_KEY to choose it. Changing it changes every code. Supported on MySQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, SQLite and DuckDB connections (it needs the sqlglot package - queryapigate[flow], in the Docker image). A caller with rules is refused on H2, JDBC and MongoDB connections, for now.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
x: Time: 30 minutes. You'll end up with: an AI client - a connector in a hosted assistant, or your own agent - connecting to your MCP server by signing its user in through your identity provider, not with an API key you hand out: the user's role decides what the agent can reach, its masking rules apply, every run is recorded under the user's name, and a token issued for anything else is refused. Stable - OAuth for the MCP server is under the compatibility promise since 0.30 (what that means). Every command and response below was run against a real MCP server and a real Keycloak 26 (in Docker), with the example APIs loaded, and a real MCP client - the Python SDK's - going through the whole sign-in: discovery, the login page, the authorization code with PKCE, the token, the tool call.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
x: AI client --(1) POST /mcp, no token--> MCP server --> 401 + where to sign in QueryAPIGate only checks tokens. Your identity provider issues them, signs the user in (with your MFA, your policies), and registers the client. QueryAPIGate never sees a password and issues no tokens of its own.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
h: Step 1: At your provider - a scope whose tokens name the MCP server
x: A token is accepted only if its audience (aud) is the MCP server's own URL - so a token your provider issues for some other application can't be used here. Make that happen with a scope. In Keycloak, in your realm: Client scopes → Create client scope: name queryapigate.mcp, type Optional, Include in token scope on. In it, Mappers → By configuration → Audience: Included Custom Audience https://data.example.com/mcp (the MCP server's URL, exactly as clients reach it), Add to access token on. A token requested with scope=queryapigate.mcp now carries: {"iss": "http://localhost:58080/realms/qag-test", "aud": ["http://127.0.0.1:5001/mcp", "account"], "sub": "7222e50f-b640-4e00-ab30-da4c0c9c9261", "azp": "agent", "scope": "openid queryapigate.mcp profile email", "exp": 1791692237, ...} (In this run the MCP server's URL was http://127.0.0.1:5001/mcp; yours is its public https:// URL.) Other providers have the same idea under another name - an API, resource or application ID URI whose identifier becomes the token's audience, and a scope on it. Whatever yours calls it, check a real token: aud must be the MCP server's URL, scope (or scp) must hold queryapigate.mcp, and sub must be there.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
h: Step 2: In QueryAPIGate - a role for agents
x: What a signed-in agent may do is a role's, as for any signed-in user: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/roles -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "agents", "connections": ["examples"], "mask": [{"column": "customer.email", "action": "hash"}] }' Give it as little as the agents need: saved queries only (a queries or collections grant, no connections) is the safest; a connection grant adds the ad-hoc execute_sql and list_tables tools, and masking hides what they shouldn't see.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
x: QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_RESOURCE_URL=https://data.example.com/mcp \ QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_AUTH_SERVER=https://idp.example.com/realms/acme \ QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_ROLE=agents \ queryapigate mcp Here, against the local Keycloak: MCP sign-in through http://localhost:58080/realms/qag-test, for tokens issued to http://127.0.0.1:5001/mcp (scope queryapigate.mcp) INFO: Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:5001 (Press CTRL+C to quit) QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_AUTH_SERVER is the provider's issuer - for Keycloak, https:///realms/. Its keys are found from its published metadata; if that can't be fetched, the log says so at startup and every token is refused until it can. QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_ROLE_CLAIM instead (or as well) lets the token pick the role: a claim holding a role name, or a list - the first that exists wins. Both URLs must be https:// (only localhost may be plain HTTP), and a hosted client reaches the MCP server from the internet: put it behind a reverse proxy with real TLS.

t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
x: The client needs a client ID at your provider. There are three ways, and which one works is between the client and your provider - QueryAPIGate plays no part: Register it yourself (any provider): create a client - in Keycloak Clients → Create client, Client authentication off (a public client, using PKCE), Standard flow on, the client's redirect URL under Valid redirect URIs - then add queryapigate.mcp under its Client scopes as Optional, and give the client ID to whoever configures the AI client. Creating clients through Keycloak's admin API or a realm import? Create the client, then add the scope: a client created with its scopes listed gets none of Keycloak's default ones - basic, which puts sub in the token, among them - and its tokens are then refused (the access token names no user). Client ID Metadata Documents: the client's ID is an HTTPS URL describing it, which the provider fetches - nothing to register, if your provider supports it. Dynamic Client Registration: the client registers itself. Keycloak supports it, but two of its default policies refuse an anonymous registration, as this run found in turn: Allowed Client Scopes (a client asking for queryapigate.mcp, until the scope was made a realm-wide optional one), then Trusted Hosts (a request from a host not on its list). Opening that up lets anyone register a client in your realm: decide it deliberately, or registe

x: | The token | Answer | So the client... | | none, or not a token | 401, resource_metadata and scope | signs the user in | | issued for another audience (your REST API, another app), another issuer, expired, unknown key | 401 error="invalid_token" | signs the user in again | | valid, without queryapigate.mcp | 403 insufficient_scope | asks for the scope | | valid, but its user has no role here, or the role's allowed_ips leave the address out | 403 forbidden | stops - signing in again wouldn't help | Tokens are kept apart. t: Let AI clients sign in through your identity provider
x: Revoking access. A token can't be recalled before it expires - keep access tokens short-lived (minutes, as providers do by default; the client refreshes them). Disabling the user at your provider stops new tokens; disabling or narrowing the role here takes effect on the next request. The resource URL is an identity, not a location: clients compare it with the URL they connected to, and the provider puts it in aud. Set it to the public URL, https://data.example.com/mcp - not the internal address the server listens on. A scope named by URI (api://queryapigate/queryapigate.mcp, as some providers require): set QUERYAPIGATE_MCP_SCOPE to it; a token carrying its last part, queryapigate.mcp, is accepted. Which person was it? The sub claim - for Keycloak, a user's ID. from_claim parameters bind to the token's claims, so a saved query can return only the signed-in user's rows.

Anything half-set stops startup, saying what's missing. Settings → Console sign-in (SSO) shows what's in use - the secret only as "configured".

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: a support agent that opens tickets by itself, and closes one only when a person has approved that exact change - each write limited to the rows it may change, run once, and on record with who asked and who approved. Stable - write tools over MCP are under the compatibility promise since 0.30 (what that means). Every command and response below was run against a real server, its MCP server and a PostgreSQL 16 tickets table, with a real MCP client (the Python SDK) as the agent - the Console at http://localhost:5098 in this run.

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
x: Agents read only, unless a saved query's author marks it for agents and the agent's key may write through it. Then it's a write tool, in one of two modes: insert - one INSERT, run at once. It can add rows, never change or remove one. approval - the first call writes nothing and answers with a link; a person approves that exact write; the agent's second call runs it, once. Either way the write runs in a transaction, rolled back if it changed more rows than the query allows.

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: Step 1: Mark the queries agents may write through
x: On the server, writes must be on (QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES=1), and QUERYAPIGATE_CONSOLE_URL makes the approval links full addresses: curl -X POST http://localhost:5098/api/v1/queries -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "file_ticket", "connection_name": "helpdesk", "description": "Open a ticket for a customer", "publish": true, "sql": "INSERT INTO tickets (customer, title) VALUES (:customer, :title) RETURNING id, status", "parameters": {"customer": {"type": "string"}, "title": {"type": "string", "max_length": 200}}, "agent_writes": "insert" }' curl -X POST http://localhost:5098/api/v1/queries -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "close_ticket", "connection_name": "helpdesk", "description": "Close a ticket", "publish": true, "sql": "UPDATE tickets SET status = '\''closed'\'' WHERE id = :id", "parameters": {"id": {"type": "integer", "min": 1}}, "agent_writes": "approval" }' max_affected_rows is how many rows one write may change - 1 unless you say more. Only one INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE can be marked - never DDL. "sql": "TRUNCATE tickets" with agent_writes: An agent-writable query must be an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE - one statement that changes data and nothing else. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and DuckDB. On MySQL, keep these queries on InnoDB tables: a MyISAM table can't be rolled back, so the row limit coul

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: Step 2: A key for the agent, allowed these writes
x: The same per-query write grant REST uses - and give the agent its own key, never an approver's token (Step 6 says why): curl -X POST http://localhost:5098/api/v1/api-keys -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "support-bot", "connections": [], "queries": [{"name": "file_ticket", "allow_writes": true}, {"name": "close_ticket", "allow_writes": true}] }' The agent now sees them as tools, marked for what they do: close_ticket readOnly False destructive True "This tool writes. A person approves each call before it runs ... It changes at most 1 row." file_ticket readOnly False destructive False "This tool writes. It only adds rows, and runs without an approval. It changes at most 1 row."

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: Step 3: It opens a ticket by itself
x: file_ticket {"customer": "acme", "title": "Monitor flickers", "idempotency_key": "chat-81-1"} -> {"status": "done", "request": "wr_ad9e595585bb", "rows_affected": 1, "rows": [{"id": 5, "status": "open"}]} Called again with the same idempotency_key - an agent retrying after a timeout - it returns the same result, and there's still one ticket 5. The same key with other arguments is refused (idempotency_conflict).

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: Step 4: It asks to close one - and a person decides
x: close_ticket {"id": 2} -> {"status": "approval_required", "request": "wr_4cfa357ce998", "approve_at": "http://localhost:5098/console/approvals/wr_4cfa357ce998", "expires_at": "2026-10-11 16:12:47", "message": "A person must approve this write before it runs. Ask them to open http://localhost:5098/console/approvals/wr_4cfa357ce998 - then call this tool again with the same arguments and approval: \"wr_4cfa357ce998\". ..."} Nothing has changed yet. The agent shows its user the link; it opens on the Console's Approvals screen (Observability → Approvals, with a count in the sidebar): who asked, the query, the SQL, the exact arguments, at most how many rows, when it expires - Approve, or Reject with a reason the agent is told. Owners and admins can decide (writes.approve); here, maria: curl -X POST http://localhost:5098/api/v1/write-requests/wr_4cfa357ce998/approve -H "X-API-Key: $MARIA_TOKEN" # {"id": "wr_4cfa357ce998", "status": "approved", "decided_by": "maria", "decided_via": "token", ...}

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: Step 5: It runs - that write, once
x: close_ticket {"id": 2, "approval": "wr_4cfa357ce998"} -> {"status": "done", "request": "wr_4cfa357ce998", "rows_affected": 1} close_ticket {"id": 3, "approval": "wr_4cfa357ce998"} -> {"error": "These arguments are not the ones approved - an approval is for exactly one write. ...", "code": "approval_mismatch"} An approval is for exactly the arguments shown, by this caller, before it expires (15 minutes, QUERYAPIGATE_WRITE_APPROVAL_MINUTES - and once approved, the agent has that long again to run it). Calling again with the same approval returns the first result: a retry never writes twice.

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: When a write would change more than it may
x: close_customer_tickets - UPDATE tickets SET status = 'closed' WHERE customer = :customer, max_affected_rows: 2 - asked for and approved for acme, who has four open tickets: -> {"error": "This write would have changed 4 rows, and this query may change at most 2 - nothing was changed", "code": "too_many_rows_affected"} It ran in a transaction, saw 4 rows, and rolled back: all four tickets are as they were. The limit is checked when it runs, so a write approved when it would change one row, and that would change hundreds by then, is still stopped.

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
h: Step 6: Why the agent has its own key
x: If the agent were given maria's token, the write it asks for would be under her name - and approving it with that same token is refused: {"error": "This write was asked for under your own name - another approver must decide it", "code": "own_write"} So a client configured with an approver's credential can't approve whatever its model asks for. Another approver must.

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
x: Every request, 30 days - GET /api/v1/write-requests/wr_4cfa357ce998: {"id": "wr_4cfa357ce998", "query": "close_ticket", "version": 1, "caller": "support-bot", "status": "done", "connection": "helpdesk", "sql": "UPDATE tickets SET status = 'closed' WHERE id = :id", "arguments": {"id": 2}, "max_affected_rows": 1, "decided_by": "maria", "decided_via": "token", "result": {"rows_affected": 1, "rows": []}} Run history, under the agent, with who approved it - GET /api/v1/history?key=support-bot: {"query": "close_customer_tickets", "status": "error", "request": "wr_27d095cbc063", "approved_by": "maria", "transport": "mcp", "code": "too_many_rows_affected"} {"query": "close_ticket", "status": "success", "rows": 1, "request": "wr_4cfa357ce998", "approved_by": "maria", "transport": "mcp"} {"query": "file_ticket", "status": "success", "rows": 1, "request": "wr_ad9e595585bb", "approved_by": null, "transport": "mcp"} And the audit log - the arguments by name and hash, never their values, since auditors read it and have no data access: {"actor": "maria", "via": "token", "action": "approve_write", "target": "wr_4cfa357ce998", "changes": {"query": "close_ticket", "caller": "support-bot", "arguments": ["id"], "arguments_hash": "5aa658ae..."}}

t: Let an AI agent write - with a person approving each write
x: What it can't judge is intent: an approver who approves without reading approves what they see. The screen shows everything the write will do except which rows - max_affected_rows bounds how many. Writes waiting raise the writes_awaiting_approval alert; unapproved, they expire. An agent with 100 waiting is refused more (too_many_pending_writes). Taking it back: unmark the query (agent_writes removed in a new version) or narrow the key's grant, and the next call - even one with an approval - is refused. execute_sql never writes, whatever the key may do. What a write returns (RETURNING) is masked like any read, for a key with masking rules. The Agents screen counts each agent's write requests by how they ended.

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: Time: 10 minutes. You'll end up with: a partner's key on a new secret, with the old one working until they've switched, then stopped. Same key name, same grants, the same history. Every command and response below was run against a real server on http://127.0.0.1:5098, with a PostgreSQL 16 orders table behind the saved query orders_by_customer (new in 0.22).

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: Before 0.22, "rotating" meant creating a second key, copying the grants across by hand, and revoking the first. The partner had an outage unless both of you switched at the same minute, the copied grants could differ, and run history and the audit log split across two names. Reissuing the secret avoids all three.

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: A key that may run one query (guide 14): curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5098/api/v1/api-keys -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "partner-acme", "connections": [], "queries": ["orders_by_customer"]}' curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5098/q/orders_by_customer?customer=acme' -H "X-API-Key: $OLD_SECRET" # [{"id":1,"total":120.5},{"id":2,"total":80.0}]

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
h: Step 2: Rotate the secret, keeping the old one for a day
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5098/api/v1/api-keys/partner-acme/rotate -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"grace_minutes": 1440}' {"name": "partner-acme", "secret": "sk_quSL2_SHS6CWDGOQMyOW6XH8q0tbiA7mfRRILykmwRQ", "previous_expires_at": "2026-10-12 18:28:43", "previous_last_used_at": null, "queries": ["orders_by_customer"], ...} The new secret is in this response only, sent with Cache-Control: no-store, as when the key was created. Give it to the partner. Until previous_expires_at both secrets work: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5098/q/orders_by_customer?customer=acme' -H "X-API-Key: $OLD_SECRET" # [{"id":1,...}] curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5098/q/orders_by_customer?customer=acme' -H "X-API-Key: $NEW_SECRET" # [{"id":1,...}] grace_minutes is 60 if you leave it out, at most 10080 (a week). Both secrets are the same key: its active, expiry, allowed_ips and rate limit apply to each, and they share one rate-limit budget - the old secret is never a second allowance. Who may rotate: anyone who may change keys (access.write - owners and admins). In the Console: API keys → Edit (the pencil) → Secret: choose how long to keep the old secret working, then Rotate secret. The new secret is shown once, and the key gets a rotating tag in the list.

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: curl http://127.0.0.1:5098/api/v1/api-keys/partner-acme -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" # "last_used_at": "2026-10-11 18:28:43", "previous_expires_at": "2026-10-12 18:28:43", # "previous_last_used_at": "2026-10-11 18:28:43" previous_last_used_at is when the old secret was last used (to the minute). Once it stops moving, they've switched. The Console's Edit drawer shows the same: The old secret works until ... · last used ....

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: Once they have switched, end it rather than waiting for the grace period to run out: curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:5098/api/v1/api-keys/partner-acme/previous -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" # "previous_expires_at": null, "previous_last_used_at": null curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5098/q/orders_by_customer?customer=acme' -H "X-API-Key: $OLD_SECRET" # {"error":"Unauthorized","code":"unauthorized"} In the Console, End now. Left alone, the old secret stops by itself at previous_expires_at. One rotation at a time. Rotating again while an old secret still works is refused, so a second click can't cut off the secret the partner is still using: {"error": "The secret this key had before its last rotation works until 2026-10-12 18:28:43 - end that first (DELETE .../previous), or wait for it", "code": "key_rotation_pending", "previous_expires_at": "2026-10-12 18:28:43"}

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: Rotate with no grace period - the old secret stops at once: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5098/api/v1/api-keys/partner-acme/rotate -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"grace_minutes": 0}' # "previous_expires_at": null In the Console: Keep the old secret working: not at all - it stops now.

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: The audit log, under the key's name, with who did it (GET /api/v1/audit?target=partner-acme) - never a secret: {"actor": "admin", "via": "break-glass", "action": "rotate_api_key", "changes": {"grace_minutes": 0, "previous_expires_at": null}} {"actor": "admin", "via": "break-glass", "action": "end_previous_secret", "changes": {"was_valid_until": "2026-10-12 18:28:43"}} {"actor": "admin", "via": "break-glass", "action": "rotate_api_key", "changes": {"grace_minutes": 1440, "previous_expires_at": "2026-10-12 18:28:43"}} Run history stays under partner-acme whichever secret made the call (GET /api/v1/history?key=partner-acme).

t: Rotate an API key without downtime
x: Several instances: every instance must run 0.22 or later before you rotate a key - an older one doesn't know the old secret, so calls reaching it with the old secret are refused. Admin tokens rotate differently: an administrator can hold several, so issue another and revoke the old one (guide 43). The encryption key for stored passwords rotates too: guide 22's Changing the key.

t: See QueryAPIGate in your traces
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: one trace from your app, through QueryAPIGate, to the database - in Jaeger here, or any backend that takes OpenTelemetry (Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog, Grafana Cloud) - showing where the time went. Experimental - tracing is new in 0.23 and its span names and attributes may change in any minor release, always noted in the changelog (what that means). Every command and result below was run against a real server (gunicorn, one worker, 8 threads), a PostgreSQL 16 orders table of 3,000 rows behind the saved query orders_by_customer, and Jaeger 2.5 as the collector.

t: See QueryAPIGate in your traces
x: Jaeger takes OTLP itself, on port 4318: docker run -d --name jaeger -p 16686:16686 -p 4318:4318 jaegertracing/jaeger:2.5.0 (In production this is usually an OpenTelemetry Collector, forwarding to your backend.)

h: Step 3: Call it from inside your app's trace
x: Your app sends its trace context in the traceparent header - OpenTelemetry's propagate.inject() does it, as do most HTTP clients' instrumentation: with tracer.start_as_current_span('GET /customers/{id}/orders'): headers = {'X-API-Key': key} propagate.inject(headers) # adds traceparent urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request( 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/orders_by_customer?customer=acme', headers=headers))

t: See QueryAPIGate in your traces
h: Step 4: One trace, end to end
x: In Jaeger (http://localhost:16686), the app's trace - here 5d1b7946cc208d89e08d0758967125e2 - has QueryAPIGate's spans inside it: shop-backend: GET /customers/{id}/orders 39.4 ms queryapigate: GET /q/ 12.8 ms http.route=/q/ status 200 caller=shop-backend queryapigate: query orders_by_customer 11.7 ms queryapigate.rows=10 queryapigate: SELECT shop 10.1 ms db.system.name=postgresql db.namespace=postgres server.address=localhost db.response.returned_rows=10 queryapigate: serialize json 0.1 ms queryapigate.format=json queryapigate.bytes=226 So of 12.8 ms in QueryAPIGate, 10.1 went to PostgreSQL. Each span records only what the list says. The parameter (acme), the statement, the API key and the database password appear nowhere in the stored trace (checked by searching it), and that holds for every span: tests fail if one ever does. From the other side: the same trace_id is in the run's history entry (GET /api/v1/history), in an error's body beside request_id, and in each JSON log line (QUERYAPIGATE_JSON_LOGS=1) with its span_id - so a slow run, an error a caller reports, or a log line leads straight to its trace.

t: See QueryAPIGate in your traces
x: 2,000 sequential requests to that query (100 rows each, one keep-alive connection, after 200 to warm up), each setting run twice: | | median | p95 | p99 | | tracing off | 3.42-3.80 ms | 5.89-6.79 ms | 6.95-9.41 ms | | every request traced | 4.50-4.79 ms | 7.28-7.35 ms | 10.85-11.63 ms | | 10% of requests traced | 3.27-3.58 ms | 5.37-5.40 ms | 6.26-6.40 ms | Tracing every request cost about 1 ms each - five spans, and encoding and sending them in the background while requests run. Sampling a tenth cost nothing measurable: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1 parentbased_... follows the caller's decision when it sends one and samples a tenth of the rest. Plain traceidratio ignores the caller's - so a client can't ask for its every request to be traced.

t: See QueryAPIGate in your traces
x: MCP: an agent's tools/call is a server span, tools/call , with the query and database spans inside it, continuing the client's traceparent when it sends one. Exports: a saved export run from the API is inside the request's trace. queryapigate export and queryapigate exports run start their own - or continue TRACEPARENT from the environment, so a scheduler that sets it (Airflow, a CI job) finds the run in its own trace. Live events: opening a stream is one span, GET /events - not one per event; a stream can stay open for hours.

t: See QueryAPIGate in your traces
x: Tracing reference - every span and attribute. Read the threat model - what goes to a collector, and who reads it. Trace a request in the logs - the request id, without a tracing backend. Wire up Prometheus and Grafana - metrics stay on /metrics.

t: Give a partner a quota and a concurrency cap
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: a partner's key that can run at most two queries at once, get at most 100 rows a call, and make 1,000 calls a day - enforced across every instance, with the partner told how much is left. Stable - quotas, like the three limits, are under the compatibility promise since 0.30 (what that means). Every command and response below was run against two QueryAPIGate instances (gunicorn) sharing a PostgreSQL store and Redis, with a PostgreSQL orders table behind two saved queries: orders_by_customer, and slow_report (SELECT pg_sleep(2), count(*) ...).

t: Give a partner a quota and a concurrency cap
x: A rate limit counts calls, not their cost. A partner under 60/minute can still run twenty two-second reports at once and hold every connection the pool has, while everyone else on that connection waits. And contracts are written in quotas - "1,000 calls a day" - which a per-minute rate only approximates.

t: Give a partner a quota and a concurrency cap
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5091/api/v1/api-keys -H "X-API-Key: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "partner-acme", "connections": [], "queries": ["orders_by_customer", "slow_report"], "max_concurrent": 2, "max_rows": 100, "quota": {"calls": 1000, "per": "day"} }' "effective_limits": {"max_concurrent": 2, "query_timeout": 30.0, "max_rows": {"page": 100, "stream": 100, "mcp": 100}}, "usage_this_period": {"per": "day", "period_start": "2026-10-11 00:00:00", "resets_at": "2026-10-12 00:00:00", "calls": 0, "rows": 0, "calls_limit": 1000, "rows_limit": null} effective_limits is what each comes to against the server's own limits - a key's limit only ever narrows them. t: Give a partner a quota and a concurrency cap
h: Step 2: Two queries at once - and no more
x: Three slow reports at once, the third on the other instance: port 5091 -> 200 in 2.02s port 5090 -> 200 in 2.05s port 5091 -> 429 in 0.017s {"error": "This caller already has 2 queries running, its max_concurrent - retry when one finishes", "code": "too_many_concurrent", "retry_after": 1, "max_concurrent": 2} The count is in Redis, so it holds across instances. A query holds its slot from when it's sent until its last row is read - a stream or a big export for as long as it runs - and each slot has a lease, so one held by an instance that crashed is freed when its lease ends. The third call isn't queued: Retry-After: 1, and the client decides.

t: Give a partner a quota and a concurrency cap
x: Two instances, clients calling as fast as they could until refused, a quota of 1,000 calls a day: | | calls answered | over the quota | | 16 clients, with Redis | 1,007 | 7 | | 32 clients, with Redis | 1,016 | 16 | | 16 clients, without Redis | 1,615 | 615 | With Redis, the overshoot is the calls in flight at the moment the quota ran out: checked before a call, counted after it. Without Redis each instance sees the others' counts only once they're written to the store and re-read - about every second - so a burst shorter than that gets nearly a whole quota through each instance. Run several instances with Redis if a quota is in a contract. One instance alone counts exactly.

t: Send the audit log to your SIEM, and prove nobody edited it
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: every administrative change signed into a hash chain, streamed over mutual TLS to your SIEM as it happens - and a check, in one command, that what QueryAPIGate holds, and what your SIEM received, is what was written. Stable - the SIEM stream is under the compatibility promise since 0.32 (what that means), as the chain itself already was. Every command and output below was run against a real server, with rsyslog 8.2604 as the SIEM - RFC 5425 syslog over TLS, requiring a client certificate - and an OpenTelemetry Collector 0.160.0 taking OTLP logs beside it: the receivers .github/scripts/siem_receivers.sh starts, the same ones CI tests the stream against on every push.

t: Send the audit log to your SIEM, and prove nobody edited it
x: python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))" # the audit key QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY= QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_LOG_EXPORT_FILE=/var/log/queryapigate/audit.jsonl # a copy on disk too Keep the key outside the store, as you keep QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY. Every audit entry is then signed with it (hmac-sha256:...), chained to the one before - someone who can write to the store but hasn't the key can't re-sign an edit. Setting it is the chain's first entry here: audit_key_set.

t: Send the audit log to your SIEM, and prove nobody edited it
x: rsyslog, taking TLS on 6514 and accepting only clients with a certificate from your CA: global(DefaultNetstreamDriver="ossl" DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile="/certs/ca.pem" DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile="/certs/server.pem" DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile="/certs/server.key") module(load="imtcp" StreamDriver.Name="ossl" StreamDriver.Mode="1" StreamDriver.AuthMode="x509/certvalid") input(type="imtcp" port="6514") template(name="parsed" type="list") { property(name="app-name") constant(value="\t") property(name="msgid") constant(value="\t") property(name="structured-data") constant(value="\t") property(name="msg") constant(value="\n") } action(type="omfile" file="/out/rsyslog.log" template="parsed") syslog-ng takes the same messages - syslog(transport("tls") ... tls(... peer-verify(required-trusted))), the parser Splunk Connect for Syslog is built on - and so do Splunk's syslog input and Sentinel's agent. For OTLP, a Collector with an otlp receiver over HTTP.

t: Send the audit log to your SIEM, and prove nobody edited it
x: QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_SYSLOG_URL=tls://siem.example.com:6514 QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_SYSLOG_CA=/etc/queryapigate/siem-ca.pem # if the SIEM's certificate isn't from a public CA QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_OTLP=1 # and OTLP logs, acknowledged per batch OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4318/v1/logs Started without a client certificate, rsyslog refuses the connection - and that shows straight away, with nothing counted as delivered, while OTLP goes on: GET /api/v1/audit/delivery {"output": "syslog", "delivered_seq": 0, "head_seq": 1, "behind": 1, "last_error": "SSLError: [SSL: TLSV13_ALERT_CERTIFICATE_REQUIRED] tlsv13 alert certificate required (_ssl.c:2570)"} {"output": "otlp", "delivered_seq": 1, "head_seq": 1, "behind": 0, "last_error": null} A certificate from a CA rsyslog doesn't trust is refused the same way (tlsv1 alert unknown ca). Add yours: QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_SYSLOG_CERT=/etc/queryapigate/client.pem QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_SYSLOG_KEY=/etc/queryapigate/client.key {"output": "syslog", "delivered_seq": 1, "head_seq": 1, "behind": 0, "last_error": null}

t: Send the audit log to your SIEM, and prove nobody edited it
h: Step 4: Changes, as the SIEM sees them
x: A key created, its rate limit changed, its secret rotated - and later deleted. rsyslog's file, as rsyslog parsed each message - APP-NAME, MSGID, structured data, the message: queryapigate audit_key_set [meta sequenceId="1"] {"action": "audit_key_set", "actor": "startup", "changes": {"entries... queryapigate create_key [meta sequenceId="2"] {"action": "create_key", "actor": "admin", "changes": {"active": true, ... queryapigate update_key [meta sequenceId="3"] {"action": "update_key", "actor": "admin", "changes": {"rate_limit": {"... queryapigate rotate_api_key [meta sequenceId="4"] {"action": "rotate_api_key", "actor": "admin", "changes": {"grace_m... queryapigate delete_key [meta sequenceId="5"] {"action": "delete_key", "actor": "admin", "changes": {"active": true, ... RFC 5424, facility 13 (log audit): the action is the message ID, seq is [meta sequenceId], and the message is the entry with its seq, prev_hash and hash - what the SIEM indexes, and what it drops a repeat by. The Collector got each as a log record - service.name queryapigate, scope queryapigate.audit - with the entry as its body and these attributes, here for entry 3: {"queryapigate.audit.seq": "3", "queryapigate.audit.hash": "hmac-sha256:9278fc6bbe80696c8f0ad6590e4aab03c7d017b207110f707878ee09c23ca466", "queryapigate.audit.prev_hash": "hmac-sha256:b318f06633e30e89d3294f920aae2f3fa6aaeaaa47b3c1733dae76face28371d"

t: Send the audit log to your SIEM, and prove nobody edited it
h: Step 5: When the SIEM is down
x: The key was deleted while rsyslog was stopped: {"output": "syslog", "delivered_seq": 4, "head_seq": 5, "behind": 1, "last_error": "ConnectionRefusedError: [Errno 111] Connection refused"} {"output": "otlp", "delivered_seq": 5, "head_seq": 5, "behind": 0, "last_error": null} Nothing is lost: each output's cursor is in the store, and entries it hasn't had are kept even past QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_LOG_LIMIT (up to ten times it). Each output is on its own - OTLP kept up throughout. 15 seconds after rsyslog started again, it had caught up: {"output": "syslog", "delivered_seq": 5, "head_seq": 5, "behind": 0, "last_error": null} More than five minutes behind raises audit_delivery_behind. With several instances, one delivers at a time - the one holding the output's lease - and another takes over if it stops.

t: Send the audit log to your SIEM, and prove nobody edited it
h: Step 6: Prove it - from the store, and from the SIEM
x: queryapigate audit verify # Intact: entries 1 to 5, keyed with QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY. queryapigate audit verify --file /var/log/queryapigate/audit.jsonl # Intact: entries 1 to 5, keyed with QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY. queryapigate audit verify --file rsyslog.log # the SIEM's own copy, as rsyslog wrote it # Intact: entries 1 to 5, keyed with QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY. --file reads what a SIEM wrote as it is: syslog lines, the entry the JSON at the end of each. Delivery is at least once, so a SIEM's copy may hold an entry twice, or out of order after a retry - an exact repeat (the same seq and hash) is dropped and counted, and entries are checked in seq order. A repeat that differs is reported (conflicting copies, naming both lines): one of the two isn't what was written. The SIEM's copy with one entry changed - the rate limit made 6000/minute: BROKEN at entry 3 (update_key, 2026-10-13 13:22:55): changed (exit 1). The store is held to the same: the server checks it every five minutes and raises audit_chain_broken at the first entry that doesn't verify - changed, removed, inserted, reordered, or re-written without the key. The SIEM's copy is what catches what the chain can't on its own - the newest entries deleted from the store, or a rewrite by someone holding both the store and the key: check the two against each other, and the SIEM's against itself, with the same command. Without the

t: Send the audit log to your SIEM, and prove nobody edited it
x: Rotating the audit key: QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_KEY=, - the first signs, both verify; startup records audit_key_rotated. Keep the old key while entries signed with it are kept. Syslog over TCP has no acknowledgement. A SIEM that closes its end, or refuses the certificate, is noticed before anything is written into the connection - stopping rsyslog with a connection open is noticed, CI checks. One that dies without closing it can lose the batch sent into it. If that matters, use OTLP logs, acknowledged per batch - or a forwarder next to QueryAPIGate. Upgrading from 0.24 chains the entries already stored and records audit_chain_started; the chain proves nothing about them before then.

t: Install on Kubernetes with Helm
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: QueryAPIGate installed by helm install - first one pod on SQLite with its store on a volume, then three pods on PostgreSQL and Redis with the events and MCP servers, changed while serving without a single failed request. Stable - the chart's values are under the compatibility promise since 0.30 (what that means). The server it installs is the same one as everywhere else. Every command and output below was run on a kind cluster (Kubernetes 1.37) with Helm 4.3, using the chart and the image of the 0.26.0 release commit, built and loaded into the cluster before they were published. Helm 3 works the same; CI installs the chart on kind on every change. The chart is published to GitHub's registry with each release, at the same version as the server: helm show chart oci://ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts/queryapigate --version 0.26.0

t: Install on Kubernetes with Helm
x: Keep the secrets in a Secret you manage (by hand here; sealed-secrets, External Secrets or Vault in production): kubectl create namespace queryapigate kubectl -n queryapigate create secret generic queryapigate \ helm install queryapigate oci://ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts/queryapigate --version 0.26.0 \ -n queryapigate --set existingSecret=queryapigate --wait STATUS: deployed NOTES: QueryAPIGate 0.26.0 is installed as queryapigate - one pod, its store on the volume queryapigate-data (kept on uninstall). See it's up: kubectl -n queryapigate port-forward svc/queryapigate 8080:80 curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/health then open http://127.0.0.1:8080/console/ kubectl -n queryapigate get pods,pvc pod/queryapigate-5fdf5f6b87-8g5tb 1/1 Running 0 4s persistentvolumeclaim/queryapigate-data Bound pvc-1b36ccd9-... 1Gi RWO standard After the port-forward, /health answers {"status":"ok","version":"0.26.0",...} and /console/ opens the Console. Sign in with the API key from the Secret. The pod runs locked down: as user 1000, with no capabilities, and with a read-only root filesystem. It can write only to /data (the volume) and /tmp: kubectl -n queryapigate exec deploy/queryapigate -- sh -c 'id; touch /x' uid=1000(app) gid=1000(app) groups=1000(app) touch: cannot touch '/x': Read-only file system

h: Step 2: What the chart refuses, and what it keeps
x: SQLite is one file on one volume, so asking for more pods is refused before anything changes: helm upgrade queryapigate oci://ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts/queryapigate --version 0.26.0 -n queryapigate \ Error: UPGRADE FAILED: execution error at (queryapigate/templates/deployment.yaml:1:4): store.type sqlite keeps the store in one file on one volume - it runs one pod. t: Install on Kubernetes with Helm
h: Step 4: Change it while it serves
x: Add a setting to values-prod.yaml (QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_RETENTION_DAYS: "30" under config) and upgrade. A pod in the cluster called /q/tables every 50 ms throughout: helm upgrade queryapigate oci://ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts/queryapigate --version 0.26.0 -n prod -f values-prod.yaml --wait Release "queryapigate" has been upgraded. Happy Helming! REVISION: 2 answered 1690, failed 0 The pods were replaced one at a time. With PostgreSQL, the chart never takes a pod down before its replacement is ready, and each pod finishes the requests it already has before stopping. Upgrading to the next release is the same command with the new --version. Upgrade one minor version at a time, and read its changelog entry first (Upgrade safely). CI runs this upgrade from the previous release to the current code with requests running, and fails on a single failed request. One pod on SQLite is replaced, not rolled. The old pod stops before the new one starts, because both can't hold the volume. Expect a few seconds of downtime per upgrade.

t: Promote a setup from dev to prod through a pull request
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: dev's connections, queries, roles and keys in a file in git; prod made to match it by CI after a reviewed pull request, all or nothing; and prod refusing changes made any other way. Stable - configuration as code, its file's format_version 1 and the commands, are under the compatibility promise since 0.30 (what that means). Every command and output below was run against two real servers: dev and prod, each with its own store and its own SQLite database of sales, with prod started with QUERYAPIGATE_CONFIG_LOCKED=1. The pull request was a branch in a real git repository; CI's steps were run by hand.

t: Promote a setup from dev to prod through a pull request
h: Step 1: Dev, as you'd build it
x: On dev, a connection, a saved query in the finance collection, and a role for partners - made in the Console or the API as usual. The connection's database is a reference, so the same file works where the path differs: POST /api/v1/connections {"name": "sales", "db": "sqlite", "database": "${SALES_DB}"} Each server sets SALES_DB to its own database. (A password is a reference the same way - ${WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD} - and a file refuses one that isn't.)

t: Promote a setup from dev to prod through a pull request
h: Step 2: Dev's setup, as a file in git
x: QUERYAPIGATE_HOME=/srv/dev queryapigate config export --out queryapigate.yaml format: queryapigate-config format_version: 1 connections: name: sales db: sqlite active: true database: ${SALES_DB} roles: name: partner connections: [] collections: finance rate_limit: 60/minute queries: name: monthly_revenue collection: finance connection_name: sales description: Revenue per month author: admin sql: SELECT month, amount FROM revenue ORDER BY month api_keys: [] Add the partner's key. A key is in a file by its secret's hash, never the secret: queryapigate config new-key secret: sk_pdiK5... # to the partner, and your secrets manager - not the file secret_sha256: 3cf3a4f9023214f61d2d657c95c1e349765d70819994ec940ebb3db012da4e0d api_keys: name: partner-a role: partner # the role's grants - kept in step with it secret_sha256: 3cf3a4f9023214f61d2d657c95c1e349765d70819994ec940ebb3db012da4e0d Commit it. Nothing in the file is a secret, so it can live in the same repository as everything else.

t: Promote a setup from dev to prod through a pull request
x: What CI runs against prod - the CLI posts the file to the server and shows its answer; the key comes from QAG_API_KEY, an owner's (only owners can apply a file): export QAG_API_KEY= # a CI secret queryapigate config diff --server https://prod.example.com queryapigate.yaml queryapigate config apply --server https://prod.example.com queryapigate.yaml The diff, on an empty prod (each object's fields left out here): connections[sales] queries[monthly_revenue] roles[partner] api_keys[partner-a] 4 to create, 0 to change. Applied - in one transaction, each change through the same rules as the API: Applied: the server matches the file (sha256 7f25ab941ccd). The partner's secret - which prod never saw, only its hash - works, on prod's own data: GET /q/monthly_revenue (X-API-Key: sk_pdiK5...) [{"month":"2026-08","amount":98000},{"month":"2026-09","amount":104500},{"month":"2026-10","amount":51200}]

t: Promote a setup from dev to prod through a pull request
h: Step 4: A change, as a pull request
x: On a branch: the partner gets 120 calls a minute, and a new query. @@ roles: rate_limit: 60/minute rate_limit: 120/minute @@ queries: +- name: best_month collection: finance connection_name: sales description: The month with the most revenue sql: |- SELECT month, amount FROM revenue ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1 CI posts what it would do to prod on the pull request - the review is of this, not only of the YAML: $ queryapigate config diff --server https://prod.example.com queryapigate.yaml queries[best_month] collection: "finance" connection_name: "sales" description: "The month with the most revenue" query_type: "sql" sql: SELECT month, amount FROM revenue ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1 ~ roles[partner] rate_limit: "60/minute" -> "120/minute" ~ api_keys[partner-a] rate_limit: "60/minute" -> "120/minute" 1 to create, 2 to change. (exit 2: there are changes.) The key changes too: its grants are the role's. A file with a problem fails this step with every problem listed, and nothing reaches prod. Meanwhile, someone tries the shortcut - the same change straight on prod: PATCH /api/v1/roles/partner {"rate_limit": "120/minute"} 409 {"code": "config_managed", "error": "roles[partner] is managed by a configuration file - change it there; this server takes changes to it only from a file (QUERYAPIGATE_CONFIG_LOCKED)"}

t: Promote a setup from dev to prod through a pull request
x: After the merge, CI applies it, then checks nothing is left over: $ queryapigate config apply --server https://prod.example.com queryapigate.yaml 1 to create, 2 to change. Applied: the server matches the file (sha256 a30e8ac0451d). $ queryapigate config diff --server https://prod.example.com queryapigate.yaml No changes: the server matches the file. Prod's audit log says who applied which file, and each change it made: 2026-10-12 16:31:22 admin break-glass config_applied a30e8ac0451d 2026-10-12 16:31:22 admin config update_key partner-a 2026-10-12 16:31:22 admin config update_role partner 2026-10-12 16:31:22 admin config save_query best_month 2026-10-12 16:30:33 admin break-glass config_applied 7f25ab941ccd ... The hash names the file's content - the same file applied anywhere has the same one - so it ties each change to the commit that holds that file.

t: Promote a setup from dev to prod through a pull request
x: Delete best_month from the file and the diff, by default, leaves it alone - it only says so: On the server but not in the file - applying leaves them alone: queries[best_month] With --prune, it's deleted - because a file put it there: $ queryapigate config diff --prune --server https://prod.example.com queryapigate.yaml queries[best_month] 0 to create, 0 to change, 1 to delete. config apply --prune then deletes it. Pruning only ever deletes what a file manages - created, changed or named by one - never what was made in the Console or the API and no file has named.

t: Promote a setup from dev to prod through a pull request
x: A CI workflow is these two steps: config diff --server on every pull request (post its output as a comment; exit 1 fails the check), and config apply --server on merge. The diff is read-only, but posts the file to the server: give both the owner key only as a protected secret. On Kubernetes, skip the CI apply: the chart's configAsCode mounts the file and the first new pod applies it as it starts (Install on Kubernetes with Helm), so Argo CD or Flux syncing the chart is the deploy. Elsewhere, QUERYAPIGATE_CONFIG_FILE does the same. Without the lock, a change made on prod shows up as drift: config diff names it, and the next apply undoes it. Run the diff on a schedule to see it. Rotating the partner's key is a pull request too: a new secret_sha256 from config new-key. The old secret keeps working for 60 minutes, as a rotation does. Use config new-key for every key's secret. A hash is safe to keep in git only because the secret behind it is 32 random bytes; a secret someone chose could be guessed from its hash.

t: Use short-lived database credentials from Vault
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: QueryAPIGate with no database password anywhere - Vault makes a database user for each lease, QueryAPIGate moves to the next one before the last expires, and not one call fails while it does; when Vault is down, it keeps serving while it safely can, then fails closed. Stable - secrets from Vault, and its short-lived database credentials, are under the compatibility promise since 0.34 (what that means). AWS's are still experimental. Every command and output below was run against Vault 1.21 (dev mode) and PostgreSQL 16, with QueryAPIGate signing in to Vault through AppRole. The leases last 60 seconds so that a few rotations fit in the guide; an hour is usual.

t: Use short-lived database credentials from Vault
h: Step 1: Vault makes the database's users
x: What Vault's administrator sets up - the database secrets engine, managing a role that may only read revenue: vault secrets enable database vault write database/config/warehouse plugin_name=postgresql-database-plugin \ connection_url="postgresql://{{username}}:{{password}}@warehouse.internal:5432/postgres" \ username=vault password=... allowed_roles=reporting-ro vault write database/roles/reporting-ro db_name=warehouse default_ttl=60s max_ttl=1h \ creation_statements="CREATE ROLE \"{{name}}\" WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '{{password}}' VALID UNTIL '{{expiration}}'; GRANT SELECT ON revenue TO \"{{name}}\";" And for QueryAPIGate, a policy that reaches exactly that - and revoking its own leases - with an AppRole for it to sign in with: path "database/creds/reporting-ro" { capabilities = ["read"] } path "sys/leases/revoke" { capabilities = ["update"] } vault auth enable approle vault write auth/approle/role/queryapigate token_policies=queryapigate token_ttl=1h vault read auth/approle/role/queryapigate/role-id # the role ID vault write -f auth/approle/role/queryapigate/secret-id # the secret ID - into a file only QueryAPIGate reads

t: Use short-lived database credentials from Vault
x: QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.example.com:8200 QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_AUTH=approle QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_ROLE_ID= QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_SECRET_ID_FILE=/run/secrets/vault-secret-id QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_DATABASE_ROLES=reporting-ro@warehouse.internal:5432 The last line says which roles a connection may ask for - and where their credentials may go: reporting-ro only to the warehouse. (On Kubernetes, QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_AUTH=kubernetes with the chart's vaultToken.enabled, and no secret ID at all.)

t: Use short-lived database credentials from Vault
h: Step 3: A connection with no password
x: POST /api/v1/connections {"name": "warehouse", "db": "postgres", "host": "warehouse.internal", "port": 5432, "database": "postgres", "credentials": {"source": "vault-database", "role": "reporting-ro"}} A saved query on it, revenue, that also says who it ran as: SELECT current_user AS connected_as, month, amount FROM revenue ORDER BY month GET /q/revenue [{"connected_as": "v-approle-reportin-8zBMUctzHI5CG3EW6P4s-1791811633", "month": "2026-08", "amount": 98000}, {"connected_as": "v-approle-reportin-8zBMUctzHI5CG3EW6P4s-1791811633", "month": "2026-09", "amount": 104500}] A user Vault made a moment ago, for this lease. Pointing the role anywhere else is refused - otherwise an administrator could have the server log in to a host of theirs with the warehouse's credentials: POST /api/v1/connections {"name": "elsewhere", "host": "db.attacker.example", ..., "credentials": {"source": "vault-database", "role": "reporting-ro"}} 400 {"code": "invalid_body", "error": "credentials vault-database is refused: 'reporting-ro' is bound to warehouse.internal:5432 by QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_DATABASE_ROLES - not db.attacker.example:5432"}

t: Use short-lived database credentials from Vault
h: Step 4: Leases come and go; calls don't fail
x: GET /q/revenue every 200 ms for three minutes - three of those 60-second leases: answered 861, failed 0 from 18:57:24: v-approle-reportin-8zBMUctzHI5CG3EW6P4s-1791811633 (179 calls) from 18:58:01: v-approle-reportin-a4lOjbOTU2pSuW4ykWGG-1791811681 (229 calls) from 18:58:49: v-approle-reportin-WwAVdOPwmARxZO2aH8m4-1791811729 (231 calls) from 18:59:38: v-approle-reportin-1dRYtNa6w8ziCcjnsNmr-1791811778 (222 calls) Four database users, each taking over about 48 seconds after the last: QueryAPIGate asks Vault for the next pair at 80% of a lease, and stops using a pair - and retires every pooled connection opened with it - a tenth of the lease before it ends (at least 5 seconds, at most 5 minutes). Every connection opened in between shares one pair: one lease in Vault, not one per connection.

t: Use short-lived database credentials from Vault
x: Vault paused right after QueryAPIGate took a fresh pair, calls once a second: 19:06:02 Vault paused 19:06:02 answered as v-approle-reportin-HCkAeIlkRnhgyui... 19:07:01 answered as v-approle-reportin-HCkAeIlkRnhgyui... (10.1s) 19:07:02 503 secret_unavailable 19:07:21 503 secret_unavailable (10.1s) 19:07:23 Vault back 19:07:34 answered as v-approle-reportin-qYgPOHrZaN6Bsso... For 48 seconds nothing changed: the pair it held was good. At the refresh point, one call waited on Vault - the 10-second timeout - and was still answered with the pair still within its time. The log says so, as a warning: The credential source vault-database failed (Vault at ... could not be reached: timed out) - using the credentials it gave before, good for ...s more. Then the pair was too close to its end, and QueryAPIGate failed closed: 503 secret_unavailable, at once - Vault is asked again only every 10 seconds, so calls don't each wait on it. With Vault back, the next call got a new pair. After five minutes of that, the secret_provider_failing alert says so, and Settings shows each provider's last answer: vault-database: ok at 19:01:55, or failing since ... with the error.

x: Leases this process took are revoked when it stops - on SIGTERM, as Kubernetes and Docker send: leases while serving: 1 leases after SIGTERM: 0 So restarts don't fill Vault with leases waiting out their TTL.

t: Use short-lived database credentials from Vault
x: A password in Vault's KV store is ${vault:secret/data/warehouse#password} in any connection field, read under QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_PATHS only - for a database that can't have users made per lease. RDS and Aurora need no Vault: "credentials": {"source": "aws-rds-iam"} makes an IAM token the password, for hosts in QUERYAPIGATE_AWS_RDS_HOSTS, over TLS only. The lease length is Vault's. An hour is usual; QueryAPIGate then takes a new pair every 48 minutes, and Vault being down is invisible for up to 54. Pooled connections are retired before their pair's lease ends, however recently used - a query never runs on a user Vault is about to drop.
